SYSTEM OVERVIEW This document serves as the primary knowledge base for a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) chatbot designed to assist users in identifying early warning signs of migraine attacks, tracking triggers, and providing evidence-based educational support. The system does **not** replace clinical diagnosis or medical treatment. ### 1.1 System Purpose - Help users recognize prodromal (pre-migraine) symptoms early - Log and analyze personal trigger patterns - Provide educational content on migraine pathophysiology - Guide users toward appropriate medical care when needed - Support medication adherence awareness (not prescribing) ### 1.2 Target Users - Adults (18+) with diagnosed or suspected migraine disorder - Caregivers of migraine patients - General users seeking migraine health education ### 1.3 System Limitations - Cannot perform clinical diagnosis - Cannot prescribe, adjust, or recommend specific medications - Cannot replace a licensed neurologist or general practitioner - Does not have access to real-time user health records unless explicitly integrated --- ## 2. MIGRAINE CLINICAL KNOWLEDGE ### 2.1 What Is Migraine? Migraine is a complex neurological disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of moderate-to-severe headache, typically unilateral and pulsating, lasting 4–72 hours. It affects approximately **1 in 7 people globally** and is classified as one of the leading causes of disability worldwide (WHO, 2016). Migraine is classified by the **International Headache Society (IHS)** under ICHD-3 (International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition): - **Migraine without aura (1.1)** — most common form - **Migraine with aura (1.2)** — involves transient neurological symptoms - **Chronic migraine (1.3)** — ≥15 headache days/month for >3 months - **Menstrual migraine** — linked to hormonal fluctuation - **Vestibular migraine** — associated with vertigo and

Key neurochemicals involved: - **Serotonin (5-HT):** Drop in serotonin levels may trigger attacks - **CGRP (Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide):** Key mediator of migraine pain; target of newer treatments - **Dopamine:** Involved in prodromal symptoms (yawning, food cravings) ### 2.3 Migraine Phases (Critical for Early Warning System) #### Phase 1: Prodrome (Early Warning — 6–48 hours before headache) This is the **primary focus of early warning prediction**. Symptoms include: - Mood changes (irritability, euphoria, depression) - Fatigue or excessive yawning - Neck stiffness or soreness - Food cravings (especially sweet or salty foods) - Increased thirst or urination - Cognitive changes (brain fog, difficulty concentrating) - Light or sound sensitivity (mild) - Gastrointestinal changes (constipation, diarrhea) - Frequent yawning (strong predictor — up to 72% of patients report this) #### Phase 2: Aura (20–60 minutes before or during headache) Occurs in ~25–30% of migraineurs: - **Visual aura:** Scintillating scotoma, zigzag lines (fortification spectra), blind spots - **Sensory aura:** Tingling or numbness (face, arm, hand) - **Motor aura:** Weakness (rare — associated with hemiplegic migraine) - **Language aura:** Difficulty speaking or finding words - **Brainstem aura:** Vertigo, tinnitus, diplopia #### Phase 3: Headache (4–72 hours) - Moderate-to-severe unilateral or bilateral throbbing pain - Nausea and/or vomiting - Photophobia (sensitivity to light) - Phonophobia (sensitivity to sound) - Osmophobia (sensitivity to smell) — in some patients

- **Language aura:** Difficulty speaking or finding words - **Brainstem aura:** Vertigo, tinnitus, diplopia #### Phase 3: Headache (4–72 hours) - Moderate-to-severe unilateral or bilateral throbbing pain - Nausea and/or vomiting - Photophobia (sensitivity to light) - Phonophobia (sensitivity to sound) - Osmophobia (sensitivity to smell) — in some patients - Worsened by physical activity #### Phase 4: Postdrome ("Migraine Hangover" — up to 48 hours) - Fatigue, exhaustion - Cognitive impairment ("brain fog") - Mood changes (depression or euphoria) - Residual head tenderness --- ## 3. TRIGGER KNOWLEDGE BASE ### 3.1 Trigger Categories #### Environmental Triggers | Trigger | Prevalence in Migraineurs | |---|---| | Bright or flickering lights | ~38% | | Strong odors (perfume, chemicals) | ~40% | | Weather changes (barometric pressure) | ~50% | | High altitude | Moderate | | Loud noise | ~30% | | Screen glare / blue light | High (modern population) | #### Dietary Triggers | Substance | Mechanism | |---|---| | Alcohol (especially red wine, beer) | Vasodilation, histamine, tyramine | | Caffeine (excess or withdrawal) | Adenosine receptor changes | | MSG (monosodium glutamate) | Excitatory neurotransmitter effect | | Tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, cured meats) | Monoamine imbalance | | Aspartame | Unclear; reported by subset of patients | | Skipping meals / fasting | Hypoglycemia-mediated | | Dehydration | Disrupts electrolyte balance | #### Hormonal Triggers - Menstrual cycle (perimenstrual drop in estrogen — most common hormonal trigger) - Oral contraceptive use or change - Menopause / perimenopause - Pregnancy (may improve or worsen migraine) #### Lifestyle & Behavioral Triggers - Sleep disruption: too much OR too little sleep - Physical overexertion - Stress (both onset and let-down/"weekend migraine") - Postural changes / neck tension - Eye strain #### Psychological / Emotional Triggers - Acute emotional

/ perimenopause - Pregnancy (may improve or worsen migraine) #### Lifestyle & Behavioral Triggers - Sleep disruption: too much OR too little sleep - Physical overexertion - Stress (both onset and let-down/"weekend migraine") - Postural changes / neck tension - Eye strain #### Psychological / Emotional Triggers - Acute emotional stress or anxiety - Excitement or positive stress - Post-stress relaxation (letdown migraine) - Depression (bidirectional relationship) ### 3.2 Trigger Tracking Logic (for RAG Model Context) The chatbot should help users: 1. Log daily triggers using structured prompts 2. Identify patterns over 4–8 weeks of data 3. Distinguish between **consistent triggers** (reproducible across attacks) and **coincidental associations** 4. Recognize **trigger stacking** — single triggers may not cause an attack, but multiple simultaneous triggers often do --- ## 4. EARLY WARNING PREDICTION FRAMEWORK ### 4.1 High-Confidence Prodromal Indicators The following combinations significantly increase the probability of an imminent attack: | Signal Combination | Predicted Likelihood | |---|---| | Yawning + neck stiffness + mood change | High | | Food cravings + fatigue + light sensitivity | High | | Sleep change + dehydration + missed meal | Moderate-High | | Single prodromal symptom alone | Low-Moderate | ### 4.2 Prediction Confidence Levels Used by Chatbot - 🟢 **Low Risk** — No significant prodromal signals detected - 🟡 **Moderate Risk** — 1–2 mild prodromal symptoms present - 🔴 **High Risk** — 3+ prodromal symptoms or known personal trigger pattern active ### 4.3 Recommended User Actions by Risk Level - **Low:** Continue normal activities; maintain hydration and sleep hygiene - **Moderate:** Consider reducing screen time, increase hydration, avoid known triggers, rest if possible - **High:** User should follow their **personal attack management plan** (as set by their physician); consider informing their healthcare provider if attacks are increasing --- ## 5. TREATMENT & MANAGEMENT KNOWLEDGE (Educational Only) ### 5.1 Acute Treatment Categories (General Knowledge) The chatbot may reference general categories of treatment — **never specific dosing or personal prescriptions:** - **Non-pharmacological (first-line, always safe to mention):** - Rest in dark, quiet room - Cold or warm compress to head/neck - Hydration (water, electrolytes) - Sleep - **Over-the-counter analgesics (general education only):** - NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen sodium) - Acetaminophen (paracetamol) - Combination analgesics (aspirin + caffeine + acetaminophen) - ⚠️ Overuse (>10–15 days/month) can cause Medication Overuse Headache (MOH) - **Prescription treatments (educational reference only — chatbot must defer to physician):** - Triptans (e.g., sumatriptan, rizatriptan) — 5-HT1B/1D agonists - Ergotamines - CGRP antagonists (gepants — e.g., ubrogepant, rimegepant) - Ditans (e.g., lasmiditan) ### 5.2 Preventive Treatment (Educational Reference Only) Preventive therapy is typically indicated when attacks are ≥4/month or significantly disabling: - Beta-blockers (propranolol, metoprolol) - Antiepileptics (topiramate, valproate) - Antidepressants (amitriptyline, venlafaxine) - CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab) - Botulinum toxin type A (for chronic migraine) ### 5.3 Non-Pharmacological Preventive Strategies - Consistent sleep schedule (same wake/sleep time daily) - Regular meals (no skipping) - Adequate hydration (2–2.5L/day minimum) - Aerobic exercise (3–5×/week, moderate intensity) - Stress management (CBT, mindfulness, biofeedback — clinical evidence supports these) - Migraine diary maintenance --- ## 6. # Anxiety & Migraine — Comorbidity Knowledge Base **Category:** Comorbidities **Version:** 1.0 | **Last Updated:** June 2026 **For:** RAG-Based Migraine Early Warning Prediction Chatbot **Evidence Base:** DSM-5, ICD-11, peer-reviewed neurology and psychiatry literature --- ## 1. OVERVIEW Anxiety disorders are among the most common psychiatric comorbidities in migraine patients. The co-occurrence is bidirectional — anxiety worsens migraine frequency and severity, and migraine increases anxiety burden. Understanding this relationship is essential for accurate early warning prediction, as anxiety symptoms can both **trigger** and **mask** prodromal migraine signals. ### 1.1 Prevalence - Anxiety disorders occur in **~50% of migraine patients** vs ~19% in the general population - Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is 3–5× more prevalent in migraineurs - Panic disorder is 3–10× more prevalent in migraineurs - Comorbid anxiety + migraine is associated with significantly higher headache frequency, greater disability, and lower quality of life - Anxiety is more strongly associated with **migraine with aura** than migraine without aura ### 1.2 Why This Comorbidity Matters for Early Warning Prediction Anxiety symptoms can: - Overlap with and amplify prodromal migraine signals (fatigue, irritability, cognitive fog) - Independently trigger migraine attacks through physiological stress pathways - Cause anticipatory anxiety about migraine (fear of the next attack), worsening the cycle - Lead to avoidance behaviors that inadvertently worsen triggers (sleep disruption, diet changes) --- ## 2. CLINICAL CLASSIFICATION OF RELEVANT ANXIETY DISORDERS ### 2.1 Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) — ICD-11: 6B00 / DSM-5: 300.02 **Core Features:** - Excessive, difficult-to-control worry about multiple life domains - Duration: ≥6 months - Associated with: fatigue, muscle tension, sleep disturbance, concentration difficulty, irritability, restlessness **Migraine Relevance:** Chronic muscle tension (especially neck/shoulder) and sleep disruption are both direct migraine triggers. Cognitive symptoms overlap heavily with migraine prodrome. ### 2.2 Panic Disorder — ICD-11: 6B01 / DSM-5: 300.01 **Core Features:** -

Duration: ≥6 months - Associated with: fatigue, muscle tension, sleep disturbance, concentration difficulty, irritability, restlessness **Migraine Relevance:** Chronic muscle tension (especially neck/shoulder) and sleep disruption are both direct migraine triggers. Cognitive symptoms overlap heavily with migraine prodrome. ### 2.2 Panic Disorder — ICD-11: 6B01 / DSM-5: 300.01 **Core Features:** - Recurrent unexpected panic attacks (sudden surge of intense fear) - Physical symptoms: palpitations, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, nausea, numbness - Persistent concern about future attacks **Migraine Relevance:** Panic attacks can mimic or co-occur with migraine aura. Autonomic activation during panic (adrenaline surge) can trigger vasomotor changes that precipitate migraine. ### 2.3 Social Anxiety Disorder — ICD-11: 6B04 / DSM-5: 300.23 **Core Features:** - Intense fear of social situations; avoidance behavior - Associated with: anticipatory anxiety, physiological arousal in social settings **Migraine Relevance:** Social stress is a known migraine trigger. Avoidance of social settings due to migraine fear can reinforce social anxiety in a vicious cycle. ### 2.4 Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) — ICD-11: 6B40 / DSM-5: 309.81 **Core Features:** - Follows exposure to traumatic event - Intrusive memories, hypervigilance, emotional numbing, sleep disruption **Migraine Relevance:** PTSD is significantly more common in chronic migraine patients. Hypervigilance and sleep disruption are major migraine triggers. Pain catastrophizing — common in PTSD — amplifies migraine disability. ### 2.5 Agoraphobia — ICD-11: 6B02 / DSM-5: 300.22 **Core Features:** - Fear of situations where escape might be difficult - Often develops secondary to panic disorder **Migraine Relevance:** Some patients develop agoraphobia-like avoidance of environments that previously triggered migraines (crowds, bright spaces, travel), which may represent migraine-related disability rather than primary agoraphobia. --- ## 3. SHARED NEUROBIOLOGICAL MECHANISMS Understanding the shared biology explains the strong comorbidity and informs the RAG model's contextual reasoning: ### 3.1 Serotonergic Dysregulation - Serotonin (5-HT) plays a dual role in both migraine pathogenesis and anxiety regulation - Low serotonergic tone is implicated in both conditions - SSRIs/SNRIs used for anxiety can have variable effects on migraine (amitriptyline and venlafaxine have evidence for migraine prevention) ### 3.2 HPA Axis Hyperactivation (Stress Response) - Chronic anxiety keeps the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis overactivated - Elevated cortisol promotes neuroinflammation and lowers migraine threshold - This is the primary pathway by which anxiety triggers or worsens migraine attacks ### 3.3 CGRP Involvement - CGRP (Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide) — the primary mediator of migraine pain — is also elevated in anxiety states - Stress-induced CGRP release in the trigeminal system may be the bridge between anxiety episodes and migraine onset ### 3.4 Amygdala Sensitization - Both migraine and anxiety involve amygdala hyperactivity - Sensitized amygdala lowers pain threshold, heightens threat detection, and perpetuates the anxiety-migraine cycle ### 3.5 Autonomic Nervous System Imbalance - Sympathetic dominance (fight-or-flight) in anxiety leads to vasoconstriction followed by vasodilation — a pattern that may precipitate migraine - Parasympathetic dysfunction impairs sleep quality (another shared trigger) --- ## 4. # Insomnia & Migraine — Comorbidity Knowledge Base **Category:** Comorbidities **Version:** 1.0 | **Last Updated:** June 2026 **For:** RAG-Based Migraine Early Warning Prediction Chatbot **Evidence Base:** ICSD-3, DSM-5, ICD-11, peer-reviewed sleep medicine and neurology literature --- ## 1. OVERVIEW Sleep disorders — insomnia in particular — are among the most impactful and frequently overlooked comorbidities in migraine management. The sleep-migraine relationship is uniquely bidirectional and cyclically reinforcing: poor sleep is one of the **most consistently reported migraine triggers**, while migraine pain and anxiety about attacks severely disrupts sleep. For the early warning prediction system, sleep data is one of the **highest-value predictive inputs** available. ### 1.1 Prevalence - **~50% of migraineurs** report sleep disturbance as a significant trigger - Insomnia is **2–8× more prevalent** in migraine patients than in the general population - Chronic migraine patients have significantly higher rates of insomnia than episodic migraine patients - In large population studies, poor sleep quality is one of the strongest independent predictors of migraine chronification - The relationship is strongest for **sleep onset insomnia** (difficulty falling asleep) and **sleep maintenance insomnia** (frequent night waking) ### 1.2 Why Sleep Is Central to This Prediction System Sleep quantity and quality data should be treated as **primary predictive variables**, not secondary context. Because: - Sleep disruption precedes many migraine attacks by 12–48 hours - Even one night of significantly reduced or disrupted sleep elevates next-day attack risk substantially - Both too little AND too much sleep are migraine triggers (non-linear relationship) - Sleep represents a modifiable, actionable variable the user can directly influence - The chatbot can provide sleep-specific early intervention recommendations when poor sleep is flagged --- ## 2. # Migraine Red Flags — Emergency Reference **Document Type:** Emergency Clinical Reference **System:** Migraine Early Warning Prediction RAG Chatbot **Category:** `emergency/red_flags` **Version:** 1.0 **Tags:** `red_flags`, `emergency`, `migraine`, `secondary_headache`, `warning_signs`, `thunderclap`, `neurological` --- ## 1. Overview Red flags in the context of headache and migraine are clinical warning signs that suggest the headache may NOT be a primary migraine but rather a symptom of a serious, potentially life-threatening secondary condition. These must be identified and acted upon immediately. The mnemonic **SNOOP10** is widely used in clinical practice to screen for red flags. --- ## 2. SNOOP10 Mnemonic — Comprehensive Red Flag Framework ### S — Systemic Symptoms / Secondary Risk Factors #### Systemic Symptoms - Fever accompanying headache (especially >38°C / 100.4°F) - Night sweats - Unexplained weight loss (>5% body weight in <6 months) - Myalgia (muscle pain), malaise, fatigue - Rash (especially petechial or purpuric — suggests meningococcemia) - Jaw claudication (pain in jaw while chewing — suggests giant cell arteritis) #### Secondary Risk Factors - Known or suspected HIV/AIDS (risk of opportunistic CNS infections) - Active cancer or history of malignancy (risk of brain metastases) - Immunocompromised state (organ transplant, chemotherapy, high-dose steroids) - Pregnancy or postpartum period (risk of preeclampsia, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis) - Anticoagulant therapy (risk of intracranial hemorrhage) - Coagulopathy or bleeding disorder - Recent head trauma (risk of subdural hematoma) --- ### N — Neurological Symptoms or Abnormal Neurological Signs - **New focal neurological deficits:** - Unilateral arm/leg weakness or paralysis - Facial droop (asymmetry) - Dysarthria (slurred speech) - Aphasia (inability to speak or understand language) - Monocular blindness or visual field defects (not typical aura) - Diplopia (double vision) - Ataxia (loss of coordination) - Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) - Altered mental status, confusion, disorientation - Seizures occurring with headache - Loss

Specific High-Priority Red Flag Conditions ### 3.1 Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH) - **Presentation:** Thunderclap headache, worst of life, ± neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, loss of consciousness - **Mortality:** Up to 50% within 30 days; survivors often have permanent deficits - **Action:** Emergency (999/112/911) → CT head non-contrast → LP if CT negative ### 3.2 Bacterial Meningitis - **Presentation:** Headache + fever + neck stiffness + photophobia (classic triad) ± non-blanching purpuric rash - **Note:** Rash is a late and ominous sign - **Action:** IMMEDIATE emergency care; do NOT wait for LP if rash present — give antibiotics empirically ### 3.3 Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis) - **Presentation:** New headache age >50, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual disturbance (amaurosis fugax) - **Risk:** Permanent blindness if untreated - **Action:** Same-day urgent care; start high-dose steroids before biopsy results ### 3.4 Hypertensive Emergency - **Presentation:** Severe headache + BP >180/120 mmHg ± altered consciousness, visual changes - **Action:** Emergency department ### 3.5 Cervical Artery Dissection (Carotid or Vertebral) - **Presentation:** Sudden-onset severe neck/head pain

Permanent blindness if untreated - **Action:** Same-day urgent care; start high-dose steroids before biopsy results ### 3.4 Hypertensive Emergency - **Presentation:** Severe headache + BP >180/120 mmHg ± altered consciousness, visual changes - **Action:** Emergency department ### 3.5 Cervical Artery Dissection (Carotid or Vertebral) - **Presentation:** Sudden-onset severe neck/head pain ± Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis), focal neurological signs - **Triggers:** Neck manipulation, trauma, chiropractic treatment - **Action:** Emergency; risk of ischemic stroke ### 3.6 Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis (CVST) - **Risk groups:** Pregnant/postpartum women, OCP users, hypercoagulable states - **Presentation:** Progressive headache, papilledema, seizures, focal deficits - **Action:** Emergency neuroimaging (MRI/MRV) --- ## 4. Red Flags Specific to Migraine Patients Even established migraine patients can develop secondary headaches. Red flags IN a known migraineur include: - Change in usual headache character, location, or frequency without explanation - Headache not responding to previously effective medications - Progressive increase in frequency/severity over months - New neurological symptoms not matching prior aura pattern - Headache triggered by physical exertion, coughing, sexual activity (if new) - Headache occurring exclusively on waking from sleep - Systemic illness accompanying headache --- ## 7. Medication-Related Red Flags - Headache in a patient on **anticoagulants** (warfarin, heparin, DOACs) — risk of intracranial bleed - Headache after **lumbar puncture** — post-dural puncture headache (postural, but also must rule out meningitis) - Headache after starting **oral contraceptives** — risk of CVST; may need to stop OCP - **Medication overuse headache (MOH):** Not life-threatening but represents a pattern change; >15 days/month analgesic use --- ## 8. # When to Call a Doctor — Migraine Clinical Decision Guide **Document Type:** Clinical Decision Reference **System:** Migraine Early Warning Prediction RAG Chatbot **Category:** `emergency/when_to_call_doctor` **Version:** 1.0 **Tags:** `doctor_consultation`, `emergency`, `urgent_care`, `migraine_management`, `escalation`, `clinical_decision`, `triage` --- ## 1. Overview This document provides a structured, tiered guide for determining when a person experiencing migraine or headache symptoms should contact or visit a healthcare provider. # Migraine FAQ — Comprehensive Reference **Document Type:** Frequently Asked Questions — Clinical & Patient Reference **System:** Migraine Early Warning Prediction RAG Chatbot **Category:** `faq/migraine_faq` **Version:** 1.0 **Tags:** `faq`, `migraine`, `headache`, `symptoms`, `triggers`, `treatment`, `prevention`, `aura`, `diagnosis`, `medication`, `lifestyle`, `pregnancy`, `pediatric`, `chronic_migraine`, `CGRP`, `triptan` --- ## SECTION 1: What Is Migraine? --- **Q1.1: What is a migraine?** A migraine is a complex neurological disorder characterized by recurrent attacks of moderate-to-severe headache, typically unilateral (one-sided), pulsating in quality, and lasting 4–72 hours. It is often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and heightened sensitivity to light (photophobia) and sound (phonophobia). Migraine is the second most disabling condition worldwide and the leading cause of disability in people aged 15–49. --- **Q1.2: Is migraine just a bad headache?** No. Migraine is a neurological disease, not simply a severe headache. It involves dysfunction of brain networks — including the trigeminal pain pathway and cortical spreading depression — and produces a wide range of symptoms beyond head pain, including nausea, vomiting, sensory hypersensitivity, cognitive impairment ("brain fog"), fatigue, aura, and postdrome. Many patients are significantly disabled during attacks. --- **Q1.3: How common is migraine?** - Affects approximately **1 billion people worldwide** (roughly 15% of the global population) - Affects **~12–15% of adults** in Western countries - 3x more common in **women** than men (after puberty) - **Female prevalence:** ~18–25% - **Male prevalence:** ~6–9% - Peak prevalence: ages **25–55** - Affects **~10% of children and adolescents** - About **2–3% of the population** has chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month) --- **Q1.4: What causes migraine?** The exact cause is not fully understood, but the leading mechanisms include: - **Cortical Spreading Depression (CSD):** A slowly propagating wave of neuronal and glial depolarization across the cortex, believed to underlie migraine aura and trigger the pain phase - **Trigeminovascular activation:** Trigeminal nerve fibers

--- **Q1.4: What causes migraine?** The exact cause is not fully understood, but the leading mechanisms include: - **Cortical Spreading Depression (CSD):** A slowly propagating wave of neuronal and glial depolarization across the cortex, believed to underlie migraine aura and trigger the pain phase - **Trigeminovascular activation:** Trigeminal nerve fibers innervating meningeal blood vessels release neuropeptides (CGRP, substance P) causing neurogenic inflammation and pain signal transmission - **CGRP (Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide):** A key neuropeptide elevated during migraine attacks; its role has led to the development of CGRP-targeted therapies - **Genetic factors:** Migraine is highly heritable (~50% genetic contribution); FHM (Familial Hemiplegic Migraine) genes include CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A - **Sensitization:** Central and peripheral sensitization of pain pathways during and between attacks - **Brainstem dysfunction:** The periaqueductal gray (PAG) and other brainstem nuclei act as a migraine "generator" --- **Q1.5: Is migraine hereditary?** Yes. Migraine has a strong genetic component: - First-degree relatives of migraine sufferers have a **2–4x higher risk** - Concordance in identical (monozygotic) twins: ~50% - Familial Hemiplegic Migraine (FHM) is a rare, directly inherited autosomal dominant form - Common migraine is polygenic — multiple genes each contribute a small increase in risk - Having a parent with migraine increases a child's risk to ~50%; if both parents have migraine, risk rises to ~75% --- **Q1.6: What is the difference between primary and secondary headache?** - **Primary headache:** The headache IS the condition; no underlying structural or systemic cause (e.g., migraine, tension-type headache, cluster headache) - **Secondary headache:** The headache is a SYMPTOM of another condition (e.g., meningitis, brain tumor, subarachnoid hemorrhage, hypertension, medication overuse) - Migraine is a primary headache disorder - Red flags (SNOOP10) help distinguish primary from secondary headaches --- **Q1.7: What are the different types of migraine?** | Type | Key Features | |------|-------------| |

# Menstrual Migraine ## Overview Menstrual migraine (MM) is a subtype of migraine that is temporally associated with the menstrual cycle. It affects approximately 50–70% of women who have migraine, making it one of the most clinically significant hormone-related headache disorders. Menstrual migraines are typically more severe, longer in duration, and more resistant to standard acute treatments compared to non-menstrual migraines. --- ## Classification and Definitions ### Pure Menstrual Migraine Without Aura (PMM) - Migraine attacks occur **exclusively** on days −2 to +3 of menstruation (day 1 = first day of bleeding) - Attacks occur in at least 2 out of 3 consecutive menstrual cycles - No attacks occur at other times of the cycle - Prevalence: ~7–14% of women with migraine ### Menstrually Related Migraine Without Aura (MRM) - Migraine attacks occur on days −2 to +3 of menstruation in at least 2 out of 3 cycles - Additional attacks may occur at other times of the cycle - More common than PMM; affects ~35–51% of women with migraine ### Non-Menstrual Migraine - Attacks have no consistent temporal relationship with the menstrual cycle > **Classification Source:** ICHD-3 (International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition), Appendix A1.1.1 and A1.1.2 --- ## Pathophysiology ### Estrogen Withdrawal Hypothesis - The primary trigger for menstrual migraine is the **sharp decline in estrogen (estradiol)** in the late luteal phase (2–3 days before menstruation) - Estrogen withdrawal sensitizes trigeminal neurons and increases neuroinflammatory susceptibility - Progesterone withdrawal may play a secondary role ### Prostaglandins - During menstruation, prostaglandins (especially PGE2 and PGF2α) are released from the uterine endometrium - Prostaglandins can trigger vasodilation, sensitize pain receptors, and lower the migraine threshold - This mechanism explains the co-occurrence of dysmenorrhea and menstrual migraine ### Serotonin (5-HT) Fluctuations - Estrogen modulates serotonin synthesis, reuptake, and receptor sensitivity

During menstruation, prostaglandins (especially PGE2 and PGF2α) are released from the uterine endometrium - Prostaglandins can trigger vasodilation, sensitize pain receptors, and lower the migraine threshold - This mechanism explains the co-occurrence of dysmenorrhea and menstrual migraine ### Serotonin (5-HT) Fluctuations - Estrogen modulates serotonin synthesis, reuptake, and receptor sensitivity - Estrogen withdrawal decreases serotonin availability, increasing susceptibility to cortical spreading depression (CSD) — the neurological event underlying migraine aura ### CGRP (Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide) - Estrogen influences CGRP expression in trigeminal ganglia - Perimenstrual estrogen fluctuations upregulate CGRP release, a key mediator of migraine pain - Elevated plasma CGRP levels have been documented during menstrual migraine attacks ### Magnesium Deficiency - Women with menstrual migraine show lower ionized magnesium levels in the luteal phase - Magnesium depletion increases NMDA receptor activity, lowering the migraine threshold ### Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Ovarian (HPO) Axis - Dysregulation of the HPO axis may amplify the sensitivity of the trigeminal pain system - The hypothalamus is involved in premonitory symptoms (yawning, food cravings, mood changes) days before the attack --- ## Hormonal Context Across the Menstrual Cycle | Phase | Days | Estrogen | Progesterone | Migraine Risk | |-------|------|----------|--------------|---------------| | Menstrual | 1–5 | Low (post-drop) | Low | **Very High** | | Follicular | 6–13 | Rising | Low | Low–Moderate | | Ovulatory | 14 | Peak, then drop | Rising | Moderate (mid-cycle) | | Luteal | 15–28 | Moderate | High | Moderate | | Late Luteal (Premenstrual) | 25–28 | **Sharply declining** | **Sharply declining** | **High** | --- ## Clinical Features ### Attack Characteristics - # Pregnancy and Migraine ## Overview Migraine affects approximately 18–25% of women of reproductive age, making it one of the most commonly encountered neurological conditions during pregnancy. Pregnancy exerts complex, phase-dependent effects on migraine — often leading to improvement in the second and third trimesters, but posing significant diagnostic and treatment challenges throughout. Understanding the interaction between migraine and pregnancy is critical for clinical management, medication safety, and postpartum risk assessment. --- ## Epidemiology - Migraine prevalence in women of reproductive age: 18–25% - Approximately 1 in 5 pregnant women has a history of migraine - Up to **70–80% of migraineurs** experience improvement during pregnancy, primarily in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters - Approximately **4–8%** experience worsening of migraine during pregnancy - First-trimester worsening is common due to hormonal volatility and nausea/vomiting - Postpartum period: **Significant relapse risk** within the first 6 weeks after delivery --- ## Hormonal Mechanisms in Pregnancy ### Estrogen Stabilization — The Improvement Mechanism - During the 2nd and 3rd trimesters, estrogen levels rise **steeply and remain continuously elevated** - This eliminates the cyclical estrogen withdrawal that triggers menstrual migraine - Stable high estrogen raises the migraine threshold by modulating serotonin, CGRP, and trigeminal sensitivity ### First Trimester Volatility - In the first trimester, estrogen levels are **rising rapidly but irregularly** - Morning sickness, fatigue, sleep disruption, and dehydration are common confounders and migraine triggers - Many women experience **no improvement** or **worsening** during the first trimester ### Postpartum Estrogen Withdrawal - After delivery, estrogen levels **drop sharply** — mimicking the pattern of menstrual migraine triggers - This is the primary driver of postpartum migraine relapse - Breastfeeding may partially delay this drop by suppressing ovulation (prolactin-mediated) ### Progesterone Role - Progesterone also rises throughout pregnancy - Its role in migraine is less clear; may have

# Exercise & Physical Activity — Lifestyle Knowledge Base **Category:** Lifestyle Factors **Version:** 1.0 | **Last Updated:** June 2026 **For:** RAG-Based Migraine Early Warning Prediction Chatbot **Evidence Base:** Peer-reviewed sports medicine, neurology, and pain science literature --- ## 1. OVERVIEW Physical exercise is one of the most powerful **modifiable lifestyle variables** in migraine management. The relationship is nuanced and non-linear: regular, moderate aerobic exercise is one of the best-evidenced non-pharmacological migraine preventives available, while sudden, intense, or poorly timed exercise can paradoxically **trigger** an acute migraine attack. The prediction system must distinguish between these two dimensions — chronic protective effect vs. acute trigger risk — for every exercise-related interaction. ### 1.1 Why Exercise Matters to This System - Regular exercisers have significantly lower migraine frequency (up to 50% reduction in trials) - Acute exertion-triggered migraine is a distinct, well-documented clinical entity - Exercise timing relative to hydration, meal intake, sleep, and known triggers determines whether it protects or provokes - Exercise data (type, intensity, duration, timing) is a **high-value daily predictive input** - Exercise deficiency (sedentary lifestyle) is an independent chronic risk factor for migraine worsening ### 1.2 Prevalence Context - ~22–38% of migraineurs report physical exertion as a migraine trigger (varies by study) - However, ~40–50% of migraineurs in exercise intervention trials experience significant reduction in attack frequency - The apparent contradiction is explained by **exercise dose and type** — the same person who is triggered by a sudden sprint may benefit profoundly from regular walking --- ## 2. (2011): 10-week aerobic program significantly reduced attack frequency and duration - Systematic review (La Touche et al., 2020): Aerobic exercise significantly reduced migraine frequency, intensity, and disability - Effect size: 30–50% reduction in attack frequency with consistent moderate aerobic training ### 2.2 Mechanisms of Protective Effect #### Endorphin & Endocannabinoid Release - Aerobic exercise elevates beta-endorphin and endocannabinoid (anandamide) levels - These act as endogenous analgesics and anti-nociceptive agents - Regular release downregulates central pain sensitization — a key driver of migraine chronification #### Serotonin Upregulation - Exercise increases serotonin synthesis and receptor sensitivity - Counteracts the serotonergic dysregulation central to migraine pathophysiology - Sustained serotonin elevation with regular training (not just acute spikes) #### CGRP Modulation - Regular aerobic training is associated with reduced baseline CGRP levels - Lower resting CGRP reduces trigeminovascular excitability and attack susceptibility #### HPA Axis Regulation - Regular exercise normalizes cortisol rhythm and reduces chronic HPA hyperactivation - Reduces neuroinflammation and lowers migraine threshold over time #### Improved Sleep Architecture - Regular exercisers have more slow-wave (N3) sleep and better sleep efficiency - Improved sleep quality is independently associated with reduced migraine frequency #### Reduced Anxiety and Depression - Exercise is equivalent to medication for mild-to-moderate depression and anxiety - Addresses two major migraine comorbidities simultaneously #### Vascular Adaptation - Regular training improves cerebrovascular regulation, autonomic tone, and reduces vasomotor reactivity - Stabilizes blood vessel responsiveness — reducing susceptibility to vasomotor migraine triggers --- ## 3. # Hydration Habits — Lifestyle Knowledge Base **Category:** Lifestyle Factors **Version:** 1.0 | **Last Updated:** June 2026 **For:** RAG-Based Migraine Early Warning Prediction Chatbot **Evidence Base:** Neurology, nephrology, sports medicine, and headache medicine literature --- ## 1. OVERVIEW Dehydration is one of the **most consistently reported, most preventable, and most underappreciated** migraine triggers. Studies estimate that **~40% of migraineurs** identify dehydration as a personal trigger. Despite its simplicity as an intervention, inadequate hydration is chronically prevalent — particularly because the sensation of thirst is a lagging indicator, meaning physiological dehydration has already begun by the time a person feels thirsty. For the migraine early warning prediction system, hydration status is a **high-sensitivity, low-effort daily input** that can meaningfully shift risk estimates and drive immediate, actionable preventive recommendations. ### 1.1 Why Hydration Is Critical for This System - Dehydration-triggered migraine can often be **prevented entirely** with adequate fluid intake - Hydration status is self-reportable and easily logged - Dehydration compounds nearly every other trigger category (exercise, heat, fasting, alcohol, caffeine) - Fluid intake can be corrected in real-time — the chatbot can intervene early - Prodromal thirst increase is a recognized early warning symptom — logging can aid recognition --- ## 2. # Daily Routines & Lifestyle Regularity — Lifestyle Knowledge Base **Category:** Lifestyle Factors **Version:** 1.0 | **Last Updated:** June 2026 **For:** RAG-Based Migraine Early Warning Prediction Chatbot **Evidence Base:** Chronobiology, behavioral neuroscience, headache medicine literature --- ## 1. OVERVIEW Among all lifestyle factors, **routine regularity** — the consistency and predictability of daily behaviors — is arguably the most impactful single variable in migraine management. The migraine brain is fundamentally intolerant of variability. Disruptions to meal timing, sleep schedules, activity patterns, medication timing, and daily rhythm are among the most commonly reported and reproducible triggers across migraine populations. The core principle: **the migraine brain thrives on rhythm and is destabilized by change.** ### 1.1 Why Routine Matters for Prediction - Routine disruptions are identifiable, specific, time-stamped events that can be logged and correlated with attack onset - Irregular routines compound with other triggers (sleep, stress, diet) multiplicatively - Regularity is a modifiable variable — the chatbot can actively reinforce it - Detecting a routine disruption is an early, actionable predictive signal ### 1.2 Biological Basis — Chronobiology of Migraine - The hypothalamus functions as the brain's master clock (suprachiasmatic nucleus, SCN) - Migraine originates partly from hypothalamic dysregulation — the hypothalamus is active in prodrome and may initiate attacks - Circadian rhythm stability directly affects serotonin production, cortisol patterns, sleep architecture, and autonomic tone — all migraine-relevant systems - Any behavior that disrupts circadian rhythmicity raises the probability of a hypothalamically-initiated migraine cascade --- ## 2. Key Principles for the RAG Chatbot When responding to interaction queries, the system should: 1. **Always recommend consulting a pharmacist or prescriber** for confirmation of specific interactions. 2. **Consider patient-specific factors:** age, weight, renal/hepatic function, comorbidities. 3. **Ask about all current medications** including OTCs, herbals, and supplements — not just prescription drugs. 4. **Flag high-severity interactions immediately** (CONTRAINDICATED / MAJOR) with clear language. 5. **Never make a clinical decision** — provide information to support, not replace, clinical judgment. 6. **Recognize that drug interactions are dynamic:** a patient starting a new medication requires re-evaluation of their entire regimen. 7. **MOH is a common, underrecognized "self-interaction"** — overuse of any acute migraine treatment worsens long-term outcomes. --- ## 11. # Over-the-Counter (OTC) Medications for Migraine > **Disclaimer:** This document is for informational purposes only and is intended to support a RAG-based clinical decision support system. It does not replace professional medical advice. Always consult a licensed healthcare provider before starting, stopping, or changing any medication. --- ## 1. Overview Over-the-counter medications are the first-line pharmacological treatment for mild-to-moderate migraine attacks. They are available without a prescription and are generally well-tolerated when used as directed. Overuse of OTC analgesics (≥10–15 days/month) can lead to medication-overuse headache (MOH), also called rebound headache. --- ## 2. Simple Analgesics ### 2.1 Acetaminophen (Paracetamol) | Attribute | Details | |-----------|---------| | Drug Class | Non-opioid analgesic, antipyretic | | Standard Adult Dose | 500–1000 mg per dose | | Max Daily Dose | 4000 mg/day (healthy adults); 2000 mg/day (liver disease, alcohol use) | | Onset of Action | 30–60 minutes | | Duration | 4–6 hours | | Route | Oral, rectal (suppository) | **Mechanism of Action:** Inhibits central prostaglandin synthesis; exact mechanism in migraine not fully established. **Efficacy in Migraine:** - Moderately effective for mild-to-moderate migraine. - 1000 mg acetaminophen shown to provide 2-hour pain relief in ~39–52% of patients vs ~17% placebo. - Less effective than NSAIDs for severe migraine. **Safety Profile:** - Generally safe at recommended doses. - Hepatotoxic in overdose or with chronic alcohol use. - Safe in pregnancy (preferred OTC analgesic). - Can be used in patients with peptic ulcer disease (unlike NSAIDs). **Contraindications:** - Severe hepatic impairment - Known hypersensitivity to acetaminophen - Chronic heavy alcohol use (relative contraindication) **MOH Risk:** Moderate — limit to ≤15 days/month. --- ### 2.2 Aspirin (Acetylsalicylic Acid) | Attribute | Details | |-----------|---------| | Drug Class | NSAID, antiplatelet | | Standard Adult Dose | 500–1000 mg per dose | |

# Prescription Medications for Migraine > **Disclaimer:** This document is intended for use in a clinical decision support RAG system. It is an educational reference only and does not substitute for individualized medical advice from a licensed healthcare professional. Prescription medications require physician evaluation and authorization. --- ## 1. Overview Prescription medications for migraine are used in two contexts: 1. **Acute/Abortive Treatment** — taken at onset to stop or shorten an attack. 2. **Preventive/Prophylactic Treatment** — taken daily to reduce attack frequency, severity, and duration. The choice of therapy depends on attack frequency, severity, disability, comorbidities, and patient preference. --- ## 2. Acute/Abortive Prescription Medications ### 2.1 Triptans (5-HT1B/1D Agonists) Triptans are the gold-standard prescription treatment for moderate-to-severe migraine. They work by binding to serotonin (5-HT1B/1D) receptors, causing cerebral vasoconstriction and inhibiting release of neuropeptides (CGRP, substance P) from trigeminal nerve terminals. **Common Mechanism:** Activation of 5-HT1B receptors on cranial blood vessels → vasoconstriction; activation of 5-HT1D receptors on trigeminal neurons → inhibition of neurogenic inflammation. #### Available Triptans (Comparative Overview) | Drug | Dose | Route | Onset | Half-life | Notes | |------|------|-------|-------|-----------|-------| | Sumatriptan | 25–100 mg oral; 6 mg SC; 5–20 mg nasal | Oral, SC, nasal, transdermal | 30–60 min (oral) | 2 hours | First triptan; SC form fastest onset; gold-standard comparator | | Rizatriptan | 5–10 mg | Oral, ODT | 30–45 min | 2–3 hours | ODT dissolves without water; useful during nausea; higher efficacy at 10 mg | | Zolmitriptan | 2.5–5 mg | Oral, nasal | 30–60 min | 3 hours | Nasal spray useful in severe nausea/vomiting; also OTC in some countries | | Eletriptan | 20–80 mg | Oral | 30–60 min | 4 hours | Higher lipophilicity; 80 mg most effective but higher side effects | |

# Migraine Anatomy ## Overview Migraine anatomy encompasses the neuroanatomical structures, pathways, and neurochemical systems involved in the generation, propagation, and perception of migraine pain. Understanding the anatomy is essential for interpreting why certain symptoms occur, which brain regions are involved at each phase, and how therapeutic targets are localized. Migraine is fundamentally a **brain network disorder** — not a localized event — involving the cortex, brainstem, diencephalon, trigeminal system, and pain modulation pathways. --- ## 1. The Trigeminovascular System The trigeminovascular system is the **central anatomical pathway** of migraine pain. It consists of: ### 1.1 Trigeminal Nerve (Cranial Nerve V) - Three divisions: **V1 (ophthalmic)**, **V2 (maxillary)**, **V3 (mandibular)** - V1 (ophthalmic branch) is most relevant to migraine: innervates the meninges, dura mater, cerebral blood vessels, and pericranial muscles - Cell bodies located in the **trigeminal ganglion (Gasserian ganglion)** #### Peripheral Sensitization - Trigeminal sensory fibers innervate: - **Dura mater** (the outer meningeal layer — pain-sensitive) - **Large cerebral arteries** (Circle of Willis) - **Pial vessels** - **Venous sinuses** - **Pericranial muscles** - These pain-sensitive structures do not contain pain receptors in brain parenchyma itself (brain tissue is insensate) ### 1.2 Trigeminal Ganglion (TG) - Pseudounipolar sensory neurons - Located in **Meckel's cave** (near petrous apex of temporal bone) - Contains cell bodies of first-order trigeminal afferents - Expresses CGRP, substance P, and neuropeptide Y - Site of peripheral sensitization during migraine ### 1.3 Trigeminal Nucleus Caudalis (TNC) - Located in the **dorsal horn of the upper cervical spinal cord (C1–C2) and caudal medulla** - Also known as the **medullary dorsal horn** - The primary brainstem relay for trigeminal pain signals - Second-order neurons here become sensitized during prolonged attacks (central sensitization) - Explains why neck pain and upper cervical muscle tenderness occur in migraine ### 1.4 Trigeminovascular Pathway

cord (C1–C2) and caudal medulla** - Also known as the **medullary dorsal horn** - The primary brainstem relay for trigeminal pain signals - Second-order neurons here become sensitized during prolonged attacks (central sensitization) - Explains why neck pain and upper cervical muscle tenderness occur in migraine ### 1.4 Trigeminovascular Pathway — Full Sequence ``` Pain-sensitive structures (dura, meningeal vessels) ↓ Trigeminal nerve fibers (Aδ and C fibers) ↓ Trigeminal Ganglion (CGRP, substance P release) ↓ Trigeminal Nucleus Caudalis (TNC) — brainstem/upper cervical cord ↓ Second-order neurons cross to contralateral side ↓ Thalamus (VPM — ventral posteromedial nucleus) ↓ Third-order neurons ↓ Somatosensory Cortex (SI, SII) — pain perception ↓ Frontal/Insular Cortex — affective component of pain ``` --- ## 2. Key Brain Structures in Migraine ### 2.1 Hypothalamus **Role:** Initiates the migraine attack (prodrome generator) - Involved hours to days before headache - PET imaging shows **hypothalamic activation in prodrome** phase - Controls: circadian rhythms, appetite, thirst, autonomic function, arousal - Explains prodrome symptoms: yawning (dopaminergic hypothalamic circuits), food cravings, sleep changes, fatigue, urination - The hypothalamus may act as the **migraine "pacemaker"** — initiating attack sequences - Connected to trigeminal system via descending projections **Subregions involved:** | Region | Function | |---|---| | Lateral hypothalamus | Arousal, appetite | | Posterior hypothalamus | Autonomic, histamine neurons (orexin) | | Paraventricular nucleus | Stress response, autonomic regulation | | Suprachiasmatic nucleus | Circadian rhythm — explains morning migraine prevalence | --- ### 2.2 Brainstem **Role:** Pain modulation, sensory processing, autonomic control #### Periaqueductal Gray (PAG) - Major descending pain modulation center - Normally suppresses pain via descending inhibitory pathways - In migraine, PAG function is **impaired** → reduced descending inhibition → pain amplification - "Migraine generator" hypothesis — PAG and surrounding brainstem structures may generate the migraine state - Contains

control #### Periaqueductal Gray (PAG) - Major descending pain modulation center - Normally suppresses pain via descending inhibitory pathways - In migraine, PAG function is **impaired** → reduced descending inhibition → pain amplification - "Migraine generator" hypothesis — PAG and surrounding brainstem structures may generate the migraine state - Contains opioid, serotonin, and noradrenaline receptors #### Locus Coeruleus (LC) - Main noradrenergic nucleus in pons - Involved in arousal, attention, stress response - Activation during prodrome phase - Noradrenaline modulates pain and sensory sensitivity #### Dorsal Raphe Nucleus (DRN) - Main serotonergic nucleus - Serotonin (5-HT) drops during migraine attack - Triptans (5-HT1B/1D agonists) target downstream receptors - DRN projects widely to cortex, limbic system, and spinal cord #### Superior Salivatory Nucleus - Parasympathetic nucleus - Controls cranial parasympathetic outflow via the sphenopalatine ganglion - Involved in autonomic symptoms (lacrimation, nasal congestion in some attacks) --- ### 2.3 Cortex **Role:** Aura generation, sensory hypersensitivity, pain perception #### Occipital Cortex (Visual Cortex — V1, V2, V3) - Origin of **cortical spreading depression (CSD)** — the basis of visual aura - Most hyperexcitable region in migraine brain - Transcranial magnetic stimulation studies confirm reduced phosphene threshold #### Somatosensory Cortex (S1, S2) - Processes pain signals from thalamus - Structural thickening observed in migraine patients (neuroplastic changes) #### Frontal Cortex / Prefrontal Cortex - Affective and emotional component of pain - Involved in attention to pain and disability #### Insular Cortex - Visceral pain processing - Interoception — body awareness during migraine - Explains nausea, GI, and autonomic symptoms #### Cingulate Cortex (ACC — Anterior Cingulate Cortex) - Emotional aspects of pain - Catastrophizing and mood effects of migraine --- ### 2.4 Thalamus - **VPM nucleus (Ventral Posteromedial):** Main thalamic relay for trigeminal pain - **VPL nucleus:** Relay for body pain (cutaneous allodynia)

Explains nausea, GI, and autonomic symptoms #### Cingulate Cortex (ACC — Anterior Cingulate Cortex) - Emotional aspects of pain - Catastrophizing and mood effects of migraine --- ### 2.4 Thalamus - **VPM nucleus (Ventral Posteromedial):** Main thalamic relay for trigeminal pain - **VPL nucleus:** Relay for body pain (cutaneous allodynia) - Thalamic neurons sensitize during prolonged attacks → **extracephalic allodynia** - Thalamus also regulates sensory gating (explaining photophobia, phonophobia) - Thalamocortical dysrhythmia may contribute to migraine interictal hyperexcitability --- ### 2.5 Limbic System - **Amygdala:** Emotional response to pain; fear of next attack; comorbid anxiety in migraine - **Hippocampus:** Memory consolidation; affected by chronic migraine (volume changes in chronic migraine) - **Hypothalamus (also limbic):** See above --- ## 3. Pain-Sensitive Structures of the Head and Cranium Not all cranial structures are pain-sensitive. Migraine pain arises from: ### Pain-Sensitive Structures (Yes) - Dura mater (especially the dural sinuses) - Cerebral arteries (especially proximal portions — Circle of Willis, MCA, ACA, PCA) - Meningeal vessels (middle meningeal artery) - Venous sinuses - Scalp arteries (temporal, occipital) - Pericranial muscles (temporalis, masseter, sternocleidomastoid, trapezius) - Skull periosteum - Orbit and periorbital tissues ### Pain-Insensitive Structures (No) - Brain parenchyma (neurons and glia themselves) - Arachnoid mater - Ependyma - Choroid plexus - Skull bone (diploë) --- ## 4. Neurochemical Anatomy ### 4.1 CGRP System **CGRP (Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide)** - A 37-amino acid neuropeptide; most potent vasodilator in the cerebrovascular system - Expressed abundantly in trigeminal ganglion neurons (especially small-diameter C fibers) - **CGRP receptor:** Heterodimer of CLR (Calcitonin Receptor-Like Receptor) + RAMP1 - Receptor expressed in: trigeminal ganglion, TNC, cerebral vessels, dura mater, brainstem, thalamus **CGRP in migraine:** - Released from trigeminal nerve endings during attack - Causes meningeal vasodilation - Promotes neurogenic inflammation - Stimulates mast cell degranulation - Increases pain signaling

Cortical Spreading Depression (CSD) — Detailed Anatomy ### Definition A slow (~2–6 mm/min) propagating wave of neuronal and glial **depolarization** followed by sustained **depression** of electrical activity across the cerebral cortex. ### Ion Changes During CSD | Ion | Extracellular | Intracellular | |---|---|---| | K⁺ | Markedly elevated | Decreased | | Na⁺ | Decreased | Elevated | | Ca²⁺ | Decreased | Elevated | | Cl⁻ | Decreased | Elevated | ### Anatomical Propagation 1. Originates in **occipital cortex** (most hyperexcitable region) 2. Propagates across cortical surface at ~3 mm/min 3. Can involve parietal, temporal, frontal cortex depending on spread 4. Cortical region affected determines aura type (visual = occipital, sensory = parietal, speech = temporal/frontal) ### CSD-to-Pain Mechanism 1. CSD → activates meningeal nociceptors via K⁺ and other mediators 2. Trigeminal ganglion activation → CGRP release 3. Meningeal vasodilation and plasma extravasation 4. Trigeminal nerve signals → TNC → brainstem → thalamus → cortex 5. Headache perceived ### Blood Flow Changes During CSD 1. Initial brief hyperemia (increased blood flow) 2. Prolonged oligemia (reduced blood flow) — up to 2 hours 3. These hemodynamic changes detectable on fMRI --- ## 6. Descending Pain Modulation Anatomy The brain has an endogenous system to suppress pain — this system is **dysregulated** in migraine: ``` Frontal Cortex / Anterior Cingulate Cortex ↓ Periaqueductal Gray (PAG) — midbrain ↓ Rostral Ventromedial Medulla (RVM) ↓ Dorsal Horn of spinal cord / TNC ↓ (inhibition ↓ in migraine) Pain signal amplification ``` - PAG dysfunction → reduced inhibition → pain amplification - Descending serotonergic and noradrenergic tracts modulate nociception - Opioid receptors abundant in PAG — part of endogenous pain suppression --- ## 8. # Migraine Phases ## Overview A migraine attack is not simply a headache — it is a complex, multi-phase neurological event that can span 1 to 5 days. Understanding each phase is foundational for early warning and prediction systems, as different phases offer distinct observable signals that can be tracked and used to predict and intervene before severe pain begins. The four canonical phases are: 1. **Prodrome** (Premonitory Phase) 2. **Aura** 3. **Headache (Ictal) Phase** 4. **Postdrome** Not all patients experience all four phases; not every attack follows the full sequence. Approximately 20% of migraineurs experience aura; the majority experience prodrome. --- ## Phase 1: Prodrome (Premonitory Phase) ### Timing - Begins **24–48 hours** before headache onset - Average duration: **6–10 hours** - In ~50% of attacks, prodrome lasts <2 hours - In ~15% of attacks, prodrome lasts 12 hours to 2 days ### Prevalence - Occurs in the **majority of migraineurs** (estimated 70–80%), though not necessarily before every attack - Often misattributed to other causes rather than recognized as migraine prodrome ### Symptoms #### Neurological / Cognitive - Difficulty concentrating, "brain fog" - Cognitive slowing - Reading or writing difficulty ← **highly predictive of imminent headache** - Speech difficulty ← **highly predictive** - Depression, irritability, mood changes - Euphoria or unusual energy #### Autonomic / Hypothalamic - Yawning (frequent, repetitive) ← **most characteristic and predictive symptom** - Food cravings (especially carbohydrates, chocolate, sweet foods) - Increased thirst and urination - Fatigue and sleepiness - Insomnia or altered sleep #### Sensory - Increased sensitivity to light (photophobia onset) - Increased sensitivity to sound (phonophobia onset) - Hyperosmia (heightened smell sensitivity) - Neck stiffness or muscle tension ← average 5.0 hours before headache - Cutaneous allodynia of scalp #### Gastrointestinal - Nausea (early) - Loss of appetite ← average 9.1 hours

Sensory - Increased sensitivity to light (photophobia onset) - Increased sensitivity to sound (phonophobia onset) - Hyperosmia (heightened smell sensitivity) - Neck stiffness or muscle tension ← average 5.0 hours before headache - Cutaneous allodynia of scalp #### Gastrointestinal - Nausea (early) - Loss of appetite ← average 9.1 hours before headache - Constipation or diarrhea - Changes in bowel movement ← average 6.5 hours before headache ### Prodrome Symptom Timing (Average Lead Time Before Headache) | Symptom | Average Hours Before Headache | |---|---| | Loss of appetite | 9.1 hours | | Sensitivity to smell | 8.5 hours | | Changes in bowel movement | 6.5 hours | | Sensitivity to temperature changes | 5.2 hours | | Muscle tension / neck stiffness | 5.0 hours | | Yawning | Variable (early, highly predictive) | | Fatigue | Variable | | Mood change | Variable | ### Pathophysiology of Prodrome - Driven primarily by **hypothalamic activation** - Hypothalamus regulates circadian rhythm, appetite, thirst, and autonomic function — explaining the diverse symptom profile - Dopaminergic activation accounts for yawning, nausea, and food cravings - Serotonin fluctuations contribute to mood changes - Early cortical hyperexcitability manifests as sensory sensitivity ### Clinical Relevance (RAG / Prediction) - Prodrome is the **primary prediction window** for migraineurs without aura - Yawning, fatigue, food cravings, and mood changes are the most patient-reportable and trackable symptoms - Early treatment during prodrome (before headache onset) can reduce or abort the attack - Triptans or gepants taken in prodrome phase show evidence of attack prevention in some patients - **Key RAG features:** yawning frequency, mood score, energy level, appetite changes, neck stiffness, sensory sensitivity ratings --- ## Phase 2: Aura ### Timing - Occurs after prodrome (if present), typically **20–60 minutes before headache** - Each aura symptom:

Trigeminal nerve fibers (Aδ and C fibers) innervate pain-sensitive structures: meningeal blood vessels, dura mater, large cerebral arteries 2. Activation triggers release of: - **CGRP** (key vasodilator; causes meningeal vessel dilation) - **Substance P** - **Neurokinin A** 3. Third-order neurons project to **somatosensory cortex** — pain is perceived #### Central Sensitization - Ongoing nociceptive input leads to sensitization of second-order neurons in TNC - Manifests as **cephalic allodynia** (scalp pain from light touch/brushing hair) - Further sensitization of third-order thalamic neurons → **extracephalic allodynia** (whole-body sensitivity) - Central sensitization is why triptans are less effective when taken late in the headache phase #### CGRP Elevation - Plasma CGRP levels are markedly elevated during migraine attacks - Return to baseline after successful triptan treatment - CGRP is both a biomarker and a therapeutic target (gepants, CGRP mAbs) ### Brainstem Structures Involved - **Trigeminal nucleus caudalis (TNC):** First relay for pain signals; in medulla - **Locus coeruleus:** Noradrenergic; involved in sensory amplification - **Dorsal raphe nucleus:** Serotonergic; dysfunction during migraine - **Periaqueductal gray (PAG):** Descending pain modulation; may be dysfunctional in migraine, allowing pain to amplify ### Autonomic Features During Headache - Nausea and vomiting (vagal activation) - Pallor, cold extremities - Nasal congestion or rhinorrhea (rare) - Ptosis or lid edema (in some) --- ## Phase 4: Postdrome ### Timing - Begins after headache resolution

# Migraine Types ## Overview Migraine is not a single uniform disorder but a spectrum of neurological conditions sharing core mechanisms yet differing in presentation, triggers, severity, and frequency. The International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD-3) provides the standard taxonomy. --- ## Primary Classification ### 1. Migraine Without Aura (Common Migraine) **ICHD-3 Code: 1.1** - Most prevalent type — accounts for **~75% of all migraine cases** - No neurological warning symptoms before headache - Headache: unilateral, pulsating, moderate-to-severe, lasting 4–72 hours - Associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia - Worsened by routine physical activity - Diagnosis requires ≥5 attacks meeting criteria **Relevance for prediction:** Harder to predict than migraine with aura since there is no clear aura signal; prodrome symptoms become the primary early warning indicator. --- ### 2. Migraine With Aura (Classic Migraine) **ICHD-3 Code: 1.2** - Accounts for **~25–30% of migraines** - Characterized by fully reversible neurological symptoms (aura) preceding headache by 20–60 minutes - Aura develops gradually over ≥5 minutes and lasts 5–60 minutes per symptom - Multiple aura symptoms may occur sequentially #### Aura Subtypes | Aura Type | Description | |---|---| | Visual aura | Most common (~90% of auras); zigzag lines (fortification spectra), scotoma, flickering lights, blurred vision | | Sensory aura | Tingling or numbness, typically starting in hand and spreading to face (cheiro-oral distribution) | | Speech/language aura | Dysphasia or difficulty finding words | | Motor aura | Weakness (see Hemiplegic Migraine) | | Brainstem aura | Dysarthria, vertigo, tinnitus, diplopia, ataxia | | Retinal aura | Monocular visual disturbances | **Typical visual aura:** Scintillating scotoma starting centrally, expanding as a crescent of flickering zigzag lines, leaving a blind spot; lasts 20–30 minutes. **Pathophysiology:** Aura is produced by cortical spreading depression (CSD) — a slow (2–6 mm/min) wave of neuronal and

ataxia | | Retinal aura | Monocular visual disturbances | **Typical visual aura:** Scintillating scotoma starting centrally, expanding as a crescent of flickering zigzag lines, leaving a blind spot; lasts 20–30 minutes. **Pathophysiology:** Aura is produced by cortical spreading depression (CSD) — a slow (2–6 mm/min) wave of neuronal and glial depolarization spreading across the cortex, followed by suppressed activity. **Relevance for prediction:** Aura is itself a strong predictor of imminent headache; automated detection of aura-like symptoms via patient input can trigger early intervention. --- ### 3. Chronic Migraine **ICHD-3 Code: 1.3** - **Definition:** ≥15 headache days per month for >3 consecutive months, of which ≥8 are migraine days - Prevalence: ~2–3% of general population; ~8% of migraine sufferers - Often evolves from episodic migraine through a process of **chronification** #### Risk Factors for Chronification - Medication overuse (analgesics, triptans >10–15 days/month) - Obesity (BMI >30 increases risk ~5×) - Sleep disorders - High attack frequency at baseline - Anxiety and depression - Stressful life events - Female sex #### Management - Preventive therapy is mandatory: CGRP monoclonal antibodies, topiramate, valproate, amitriptyline - Botulinum toxin (onabotulinumtoxin A) — FDA-approved specifically for chronic migraine - Withdrawal of overused medications --- ### 4. Episodic Migraine - **Definition:** <15 headache days per month - Subdivided into: - **Low-frequency episodic:** <10 days/month - **High-frequency episodic:** 10–14 days/month (higher risk of chronification) - Standard acute treatment approach --- ## Specialized Migraine Types ### 5. Hemiplegic Migraine **ICHD-3 Codes: 1.2.3 (Familial), 1.2.4 (Sporadic)** - Rare; characterized by **motor weakness (hemiplegia)** as part of the aura - Motor weakness must be fully reversible - Can last hours to days - Other aura features (visual, sensory, speech) co-occur **Genetic subtypes (Familial Hemiplegic Migraine - FHM):** | Subtype | Gene | Protein | |---|---|---| | FHM1 | CACNA1A |

Vestibular Migraine (Migraine-Associated Vertigo) **ICHD-3 Code: A1.6.5** - Characterized by episodic vestibular symptoms (vertigo, dizziness, imbalance) associated with migraine - Vertigo episodes last 5 minutes to 72 hours - One of the most common causes of episodic vertigo in adults - May occur with or without headache during the episode - Diagnosis requires history of migraine AND current vestibular symptoms --- ### 7. Menstrual Migraine **ICHD-3 Code: A1.1.1 / A1.2.0.1** - Triggered by the drop in estrogen just before menstruation - **Pure menstrual migraine:** Occurs exclusively during menstruation (within 2 days before to 3 days after onset), in at least 2 of 3 cycles - **Menstrually related migraine:** Occurs during menstruation but also at other times - Often more severe, longer-lasting, and more resistant to treatment than non-menstrual attacks - Management: perimenstrual preventive therapy (frovatriptan, naproxen, transdermal estrogen) --- ### 8. Retinal Migraine (Ocular Migraine) **ICHD-3 Code: 1.2.6** - Repeated attacks of monocular (one eye) visual disturbance including scintillations, scotoma, or blindness - Associated with ipsilateral headache - Reversible within 60 minutes - Rare; important to distinguish from amaurosis fugax (TIA) or retinal artery occlusion --- ### 9. Silent Migraine (Acephalgic Migraine / Migraine Without Headache) - Aura symptoms occur **without headache** - Visual disturbances, sensory changes, speech difficulties, or other aura symptoms present - More common in older adults; may represent evolution of typical migraine - Important: first-time aura without headache must be evaluated to rule out TIA --- ### 10. Abdominal Migraine (Pediatric) **ICHD-3 Code: 1.6.1** - Primarily affects children (aged 5–12) - Recurrent episodes of moderate-to-severe midline abdominal pain lasting 2–72 hours - Associated with nausea, vomiting, pallor, anorexia - No headache required for diagnosis - Strong family history of migraine - Often precedes development of typical migraine in adulthood - Part of **migraine equivalents** or **childhood periodic syndromes** --- ### 11. # What Is Migraine ## Overview Migraine is a genetically influenced, complex neurological disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of moderate-to-severe headache, typically unilateral and pulsating, frequently accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and heightened sensitivity to light (photophobia) and sound (phonophobia). It is far more than a bad headache — it is a brain network disorder with distinct neurobiological mechanisms. - **Global prevalence:** ~12–16% of the worldwide population; affects approximately 1.1 billion people - **Sex distribution:** 3× more common in women than men (post-puberty), largely due to hormonal influences - **Onset:** Most commonly begins between ages 10 and 40 - **Chronicity:** Can be episodic or chronic; attacks last 4 to 72 hours if untreated - **Disability:** Ranked among the top causes of years lived with disability globally (WHO) --- ## Definition and Classification ### ICD / ICHD Criteria (International Classification of Headache Disorders) Migraine without aura (ICHD-3 1.1): - At least 5 attacks lasting 4–72 hours - At least 2 of: unilateral location, pulsating quality, moderate/severe intensity, aggravated by routine activity - At least 1 of: nausea/vomiting, photophobia AND phonophobia Migraine with aura (ICHD-3 1.2): - All of the above PLUS at least one fully reversible aura symptom (visual, sensory, speech/language, motor, brainstem, retinal) - Aura lasts 5–60 minutes, spreads gradually --- ## Core Characteristics | Feature | Detail | |---|---| | Pain location | Unilateral (one-sided) in ~60% of cases; can be bilateral | | Pain quality | Throbbing, pulsating | | Pain intensity | Moderate to severe (often 6–10/10) | | Duration (untreated) | 4–72 hours | | Associated symptoms | Nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, osmophobia | | Aggravating factors | Physical activity, bright light, loud noise, strong odors | | Relieving factors | Rest in dark quiet room, sleep, cold compresses | --- ## Neurobiological Nature Migraine is now

| Duration (untreated) | 4–72 hours | | Associated symptoms | Nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, osmophobia | | Aggravating factors | Physical activity, bright light, loud noise, strong odors | | Relieving factors | Rest in dark quiet room, sleep, cold compresses | --- ## Neurobiological Nature Migraine is now understood as a **neurovascular disorder** — not purely vascular or purely neural, but involving a complex interplay between: - **Cortical hyperexcitability:** The migraine brain is inherently more excitable between attacks; reduced habituation to sensory stimuli - **Trigeminovascular activation:** The trigeminal nerve innervates pain-sensitive meningeal and cerebral blood vessels; its activation releases CGRP and other inflammatory neuropeptides - **Central sensitization:** During attacks, central pain pathways become sensitized, producing allodynia (pain from normally non-painful stimuli, e.g., brushing hair) - **Brainstem and hypothalamic involvement:** Imaging studies show activation of brainstem nuclei and the hypothalamus even before headache starts --- ## Genetic Basis - Migraine has a strong hereditary component; ~50% heritability estimated - Multiple susceptibility genes identified (polygenic disorder) - Familial hemiplegic migraine (FHM) is a rare monogenic subtype caused by mutations in CACNA1A (calcium channel), ATP1A2 (sodium-potassium pump), or SCN1A (sodium channel) - These mutations reveal that ion channel dysfunction and cortical excitability are central mechanisms --- ## Key Neurotransmitters and Neuropeptides | Substance | Role in Migraine | |---|---| | CGRP (Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide) | Primary vasodilatory neuropeptide; markedly elevated during attacks; key therapeutic target | | Serotonin (5-HT) | Drops during attack; triptans work via 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonism | | Substance P | Co-released with CGRP; promotes neurogenic inflammation | | Glutamate | Excitatory neurotransmitter; involved in cortical spreading depression | | Dopamine | Prodrome symptoms (yawning, nausea, food cravings) linked to dopaminergic activation | | Nitric oxide (NO) | Potent vasodilator; triggers migraine in susceptible individuals | --- ##

Detailed headache history (frequency, duration, character, location, associated symptoms) 2. Neurological examination 3. Screening for red flags (to rule out secondary headaches): - Sudden thunderclap onset ("worst headache of life") - Progressive worsening over days/weeks - New headache in patient >50 years - Headache with fever, stiff neck, rash - Headache with focal neurological deficit - Headache after head trauma ### Diagnostic Tools - **Headache diary:** Gold standard for pattern recognition and trigger identification - **MIDAS scale:** Migraine Disability Assessment Score - **HIT-6:** Headache Impact Test --- ## Treatment Overview ### Acute (Abortive) Treatment - **NSAIDs:** Ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin (first-line for mild-moderate) - **Triptans:** Sumatriptan, rizatriptan, eletriptan

Overview: Hydration and Migraine Dehydration is one of the most consistently reported and rapidly acting migraine triggers, recognized by the International Headache Society. Even mild dehydration (1–2% body weight loss) is sufficient to initiate or worsen migraine attacks in susceptible individuals. The mechanism is multifactorial — intracranial fluid shifts, electrolyte imbalance, plasma osmolarity changes, and sympathetic nervous system activation all contribute. **Key clinical facts:** - Dehydration is reported as a trigger by 33–40% of migraine patients - Migraine attacks are associated with a 12–15% increase in urine output (due to autonomic dysregulation during attack) - Adequate hydration reduces migraine frequency by 21% and severity by 22% in controlled studies - Prodromal phase can include increased thirst — early warning signal - Attack-related nausea and vomiting worsen dehydration, creating a self-perpetuating loop --- ## 2. Physiology of Dehydration-Triggered Migraine ### Mechanisms 1. **Plasma hyperosmolarity:** Reduced fluid volume → increased plasma osmolarity → osmoreceptors in hypothalamus activate → trigeminal sensitization 2. **Intracranial fluid shifts:** Dehydration reduces CSF volume → increased meningeal traction → dural stretch → trigeminal activation 3. **Cerebral blood flow reduction:** Dehydration causes vasoconstriction → subsequent compensatory vasodilation → throbbing headache 4. **Electrolyte imbalance:** Loss of sodium, potassium, magnesium → neuronal hyperexcitability → lowered migraine threshold 5. **Cortisol elevation:** Dehydration stress → hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis activation → cortisol spike → serotonin dysregulation 6. **Reduced serotonin:** Serotonin synthesis requires adequate hydration; dehydration lowers 5-HT availability → trigeminovascular activation ### Threshold for Migraine Trigger | Dehydration Level | Body Weight Loss | Symptoms | Migraine Risk | |------------------|-----------------|----------|---------------| |

Overview: Meal Patterns and Migraine Irregular eating patterns are among the most modifiable and underappreciated migraine triggers. Meal skipping, prolonged fasting, large glycemic spikes followed by crashes, and inconsistent meal timing all disrupt metabolic homeostasis in ways that directly lower migraine threshold. The hypothalamus — the brain's metabolic regulation center — is also central to migraine pathogenesis, creating a direct anatomical link between nutrition behavior and headache biology. **Key clinical facts:** - Meal skipping / fasting is reported as a migraine trigger by 57% of patients — one of the most common triggers - Hypoglycemia (blood glucose < 70 mg/dL) directly activates nociceptive pathways - Migraine attacks are 2–3× more likely on days with a skipped meal vs. days with regular meals - Regular meal timing (within ±30 min of usual time) reduces migraine frequency by up to 30% - Caloric restriction without medical supervision worsens migraine in susceptible individuals --- ## 2. vasoconstriction → compensatory vasodilation → throbbing headache 5. **Neuronal energy deficit:** Brain consumes ~20% of total body glucose; neurons in trigeminal nucleus are sensitive to glucose fluctuations 6. **Neuropeptide Y release:** Fasting activates NPY pathways in hypothalamus → modulates pain processing and increases susceptibility to CSD 7. **Serotonin drop:** Fasting reduces tryptophan availability → reduced 5-HT synthesis → trigeminovascular activation ### Blood Glucose Thresholds | Blood Glucose Level | Status | Migraine Risk | |--------------------|--------|---------------| | > 100 mg/dL | Normal (fasting) | Low | | 80–100 mg/dL | Low-normal | Low | | 70–80 mg/dL | Borderline | Low-Moderate | | 54–70 mg/dL | Mild hypoglycemia | **HIGH** | | < 54 mg/dL | Severe hypoglycemia | **VERY HIGH** + other neurological symptoms | ### Reactive Hypoglycemia - Occurs 1–4 hours after a large high-glycemic meal - Blood glucose spikes → insulin surge → glucose overcorrection → hypoglycemia - Common with refined carbohydrate meals (white bread, sugary drinks, candy) - Triggers migraine more insidiously than frank fasting hypoglycemia - Symptoms: sweating, shakiness, hunger, headache 2–3 hours post-meal --- ## 3. # Trigger Foods — Knowledge Base for Migraine Early Warning RAG System ## Document Metadata - **Domain:** Nutrition / Neurology - **Purpose:** RAG knowledge base for migraine early warning prediction - **Tags:** trigger foods, tyramine, histamine, MSG, nitrates, aspartame, food triggers, dietary migraine, phenylethylamine --- ## 1. Overview: Food Triggers and Migraine Dietary triggers account for approximately 20–30% of migraine attacks in susceptible individuals. Food triggers do not act uniformly — the same food may trigger an attack in one person but not another, and may trigger an attack one day but not another in the same person. This variability reflects the cumulative "trigger threshold" model: migraine occurs when the sum of active triggers exceeds an individual's threshold, which varies daily. **Key clinical facts:** - ~20–30% of migraineurs identify at least one food trigger - Alcohol and caffeine are the most consistently identified dietary triggers - Food triggers typically cause migraine within 30 minutes to 12 hours of consumption - Delayed reactions (6–12 hours) are common and make identification difficult - Trigger sensitivity increases when food triggers combine with other triggers (stress, hormones, poor sleep) - Elimination of suspected triggers reduces migraine frequency in ~50% of patients who try it - Perceived food triggers may sometimes reflect cravings during the migraine prodrome (the food is not the trigger — the prodrome is) --- ## 2. The Threshold Model of Migraine Triggers Food triggers rarely act in isolation. The migraine threshold is a dynamic concept: ``` Migraine Threshold (variable) = Biological resilience - (Sum of active triggers) When: Sum of triggers > Current threshold → MIGRAINE ATTACK ``` **Implications for RAG:** - A food that "sometimes" triggers migraine is operating near threshold - Same food + additional trigger (stress, poor sleep, hormonal change) → attack more likely - Trigger stacking: 2–3

Food Trigger Diary Methodology ### Tracking Format For each meal/snack, record: 1. Foods consumed (specific, not just "salad") 2. Time of consumption 3. Hours since last meal 4. Hydration status 5. Other concurrent triggers (stress, sleep, hormonal phase) 6. Headache onset time (if any) 7. Time gap: food → headache onset ### Identifying True Triggers vs. Confounders - **True trigger:** Consistent relationship; headache within 30 min–12 hours; reproducible on challenge - **Prodrome craving:** Food consumed 1–6 hours before attack begins; craving was part of early attack (not causal) - **Coincidence:** Food consumed same day as attack; no temporal or reproducible pattern - **Elimination challenge:** Remove food for 4–6 weeks; reintroduce; compare headache frequency ### LEAP (Lifestyle, Eating, and Activity Plan) Method - Systematic elimination and reintroduction of 6 most common dietary triggers - Phase 1 (weeks 1–4): Eliminate all 6 categories simultaneously - Phase 2 (weeks 5–10): Reintroduce one category per week, monitoring for 72 hours - Record: headache frequency and severity before vs. during each phase --- ## 12.
