# Sleep Disorders — Knowledge Base for Migraine Early Warning RAG System ## Document Metadata - **Domain:** Sleep Medicine / Neurology - **Purpose:** RAG knowledge base for migraine early warning prediction - **Tags:** sleep disorders, insomnia, sleep apnea, circadian rhythm disorder, migraine comorbidity, REM disorder --- ## 1. Overview: Sleep Disorders and Migraine Sleep disorders represent a major class of migraine comorbidities and bidirectional triggers. Approximately 50% of chronic migraine patients have a concurrent diagnosable sleep disorder. Sleep disorders impair the restorative processes that keep migraine threshold high, and migraine pain itself perpetuates sleep fragmentation, creating a reinforcing cycle. **Core clinical facts:** - Sleep disorders increase migraine attack frequency by 2–8× depending on disorder severity - Treating comorbid sleep disorders reduces migraine days per month by an average of 30–50% - Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) alone is present in ~36% of chronic migraine patients vs. ~14% of general population - Morning headache is the most common symptom overlap between sleep disorders and migraine --- ## 2. Insomnia Disorder ### Definition Difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, or early morning awakening, occurring ≥ 3 nights/week for ≥ 3 months, with daytime impairment. Not better explained by another sleep or medical disorder. ### Subtypes - **Sleep onset insomnia:** Difficulty falling asleep (latency > 30 min) - **Sleep maintenance insomnia:** Frequent awakening, WASO > 60 min - **Early morning awakening insomnia:** Waking > 30 min before desired time - **Mixed insomnia:** Combination of above (most common in migraine patients) ### Insomnia–Migraine Relationship - Insomnia is present in ~50% of episodic and ~80% of chronic migraine patients - Hyperarousal (elevated nocturnal cortisol, elevated sympathetic tone) is shared mechanism - Insomnia increases allodynia (skin sensitivity) — a marker of central sensitization in migraine - Each additional night of insomnia increases next-day migraine probability by ~17% -

Diagnosed by AHI (Apnea-Hypopnea Index): - Mild: AHI 5–14 events/hour - Moderate: AHI 15–29 events/hour - Severe: AHI ≥ 30 events/hour ### OSA–Migraine Relationship - Morning headache is a cardinal symptom of OSA (mechanism: nocturnal hypercapnia + cerebral vasodilation) - OSA-related morning headache can be indistinguishable from migraine; differentiating via

Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS) and Periodic Limb Movement Disorder (PLMD) ### RLS Definition Urge to move legs, usually with uncomfortable sensations, that: - Worsens at rest/inactivity - Partially relieved by movement - Worse in the evening/night - Not explained by another behavioral or medical condition ### RLS–Migraine Relationship - RLS prevalence in migraine patients: ~17–24% vs. ~7% in general population - Shared pathophysiology: dopaminergic dysfunction + iron deficiency - Serum ferritin < 50 ng/mL associated with both RLS severity and migraine frequency - RLS disrupts sleep onset and early NREM sleep → reduces restorative sleep → increases migraine risk - Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) treat RLS and may modulate migraine via dopaminergic pathways ### PLMD - Rhythmic limb movements during sleep (NREM) causing arousals - Often co-occurs with RLS - Causes sleep fragmentation → reduced N3 → elevated pain threshold lowering **RAG Predictive Signal:** - Reported leg discomfort at night/restlessness → RLS flag; iron deficiency + migraine co-risk - Partner reporting repetitive leg movements during sleep → PLMD flag --- ## 5. Overview of Sleep Hygiene Sleep hygiene refers to a set of behavioral and environmental practices designed to promote consistent, high-quality sleep. # Migraine Diary ## Overview A migraine diary is a structured, longitudinal self-monitoring tool used to record migraine attacks and related variables over time. It is the gold standard for diagnosing migraine subtypes, identifying personal triggers, evaluating treatment response, and generating the temporal data needed for pattern recognition and early warning prediction. In a RAG-based migraine early warning system, diary entries represent the primary patient-generated dataset for model training and real-time inference. --- ## Purpose and Clinical Utility - **Diagnosis confirmation:** Enables retrospective review of attack frequency, duration, and features to confirm ICHD-3 criteria - **Trigger identification:** Correlates attack onset with preceding activities, foods, sleep, stress, and environmental conditions - **Treatment tracking:** Monitors acute medication use, efficacy, and overuse patterns (medication overuse headache risk) - **Hormonal correlation:** Links attacks to menstrual cycle phases (essential for menstrual migraine classification) - **Disability assessment:** Provides data for MIDAS and HIT-6 scoring - **Predictive modeling:** Time-series diary data is the core input for early warning algorithms --- ## Standard Migraine Diary Components ### 1. # Pattern Analysis in Migraine Early Warning Prediction ## Overview Pattern analysis in migraine refers to the systematic identification of recurring temporal, physiological, behavioral, and environmental patterns that precede migraine attacks. It transforms raw symptom and diary data into actionable, personalized predictive signals. For a RAG-based early warning system, pattern analysis defines the features, relationships, and decision rules the system uses to anticipate attacks — enabling timely intervention before headache onset. --- ## Why Pattern Analysis Is Central to Migraine Prediction - **Migraine is not random:** Attacks follow identifiable biological rhythms and personalized trigger combinations - **Individual variability is high:** Population-level triggers differ significantly from individual-level triggers - **Prodrome window is time-limited:** Early warning is only useful if the prediction is made ≥6 hours before attack — pattern recognition defines that window - **Multi-factorial:** No single feature reliably predicts an attack; pattern analysis integrates multiple signals into a composite prediction --- ## Types of Patterns in Migraine ### 1. Temporal Patterns #### Attack Frequency Patterns - **Episodic migraine:** <15 headache days/month - **High-frequency episodic:** 10–14 headache days/month - **Chronic migraine:** ≥15 headache days/month, of which ≥8 are migraine, for ≥3 months - **Transformed migraine:** Gradual increase from episodic to chronic — early pattern detection critical #### Circadian (Time-of-Day) Patterns - Peak attack onset: early morning (4–9 AM) — most common - Associated with REM sleep rebound, cortisol nadir, and serotonin trough - Second peak: afternoon (~3–6 PM) - Fewer attacks during sleep in most patients - "Alarm clock" headache: waking with migraine — consider sleep apnea, cluster headache #### Day-of-Week Patterns - **"Weekend migraine" / "Let-down" migraine:** Occurs Friday evening / Saturday morning - Mechanism: Cortisol drop after work-week stress; caffeine withdrawal; sleep schedule change; oversleeping - Identification: 3+ events on same day of week over 3 months = day-of-week

with migraine — consider sleep apnea, cluster headache #### Day-of-Week Patterns - **"Weekend migraine" / "Let-down" migraine:** Occurs Friday evening / Saturday morning - Mechanism: Cortisol drop after work-week stress; caffeine withdrawal; sleep schedule change; oversleeping - Identification: 3+ events on same day of week over 3 months = day-of-week pattern #### Monthly / Menstrual Patterns (Women) - Map attacks to menstrual cycle day (day 1 = first day of menstruation) - **High-risk window:** Day −2 to +3 (perimenstrual window) - **Secondary peak:** Ovulatory (day ~14) — mid-cycle estrogen surge then drop - Calculate: Proportion of attacks in perimenstrual window vs. rest of cycle - ≥2/3 cycles with perimenstrual attacks = Menstrually Related Migraine classification #### Seasonal Patterns - Some patients have higher attack frequency in specific seasons - Summer: Heat, dehydration, barometric instability - Spring/Autumn: Rapid weather changes, allergen triggers - Winter: Low light, altered sleep cycles - Track: Monthly attack rate over 12+ months #### Annual/Long-Term Trends - Attack frequency trends over years (worsening, stable, improving) - Correlation with life events: pregnancy, menopause, stress events, new medications - Medication overuse development pattern --- ### 2. Rank symptoms by hit rate and specificity (appears before attacks but not on non-attack days) 5. Trigger Patterns #### Trigger Frequency Analysis - For each suspected trigger, calculate: - **Prevalence rate:** % of attacks preceded by this trigger in prior 24–48h - **Base rate:** % of all days when this trigger is present (trigger-day frequency) - **Positive Predictive Value (PPV):** P(attack | trigger present) - **Attributable Risk:** Excess attack rate on trigger days vs. non-trigger days #### Common Trigger Categories and Population Prevalence | Trigger | Approximate Prevalence in Migraineurs | |---|---| | Stress / psychological tension | 50–80% | | Sleep deprivation | 50–75% | | Menstrual cycle (women) | 50–70% | | Weather / barometric pressure change | 40–60% | | Skipped meals / fasting | 40–60% | | Dehydration | 40–55% | | Alcohol (especially red wine) | 35–50% | | Bright or flickering light | 30–50% | | Oversleeping | 25–50% |

Time Series Analysis #### Rolling Attack Frequency - 30-day rolling window attack count - Identifies trends: increasing (risk of chronification), stable, decreasing (treatment response) - Seasonality decomposition (STL decomposition) for annual patterns #### Autocorrelation Analysis - Identifies periodic patterns in attack occurrence (e.g., 28-day menstrual cycle) - Lag correlations between trigger variables and attack occurrence - Use: ACF/PACF plots on daily attack binary (0/1) time series #### Cross-Correlation Analysis - Correlation between trigger variable (e.g., sleep hours) and attack occurrence at different lag times - Identifies optimal prediction window for each trigger ### 2. # Symptom Tracking in Migraine ## Overview Symptom tracking is the systematic, time-stamped recording of all migraine-related symptoms across all four phases of the migraine attack cycle — prodrome, aura, headache (ictal), and postdrome. Unlike simple headache diaries that focus on attack-level data, comprehensive symptom tracking captures the full biological signature of each migraine episode. This granular data enables detection of pre-attack warning patterns, personalized early warning thresholds, and phase-specific clinical decision support in a RAG-based prediction system. --- ## The Four Phases of Migraine — Symptom Framework ### Phase 1: Prodrome (Premonitory Phase) **Timing:** 6–72 hours before headache onset (mean: ~24 hours) **Prevalence:** Experienced by 30–80% of migraineurs The prodrome is the most clinically important phase for early warning systems. Symptoms arise from hypothalamic activation and altered dopaminergic/serotonergic signaling before trigeminal activation occurs. #### Prodrome Symptoms Catalogue **Neurological / Cognitive** - Difficulty concentrating ("brain fog") - Cognitive slowing - Memory lapses - Word-finding difficulty - Reading difficulty - Heightened sensory perception (before frank photophobia) - Derealization or feeling "not quite right" **Mood / Psychological** - Irritability (most common mood prodrome) - Depression / low mood - Anxiety, restlessness - Euphoria / hyperactivity (less common but documented) - Social withdrawal - Emotional lability **Autonomic / Vegetative** - Yawning (repetitive, uncontrolled — highly specific prodrome marker) - Fatigue / excessive tiredness - Pallor or flushing - Increased urination (polyuria) - Fluid retention / bloating - Changes in bowel habits (constipation or diarrhea) - Increased thirst - Nasal congestion or rhinorrhea **Musculoskeletal** - Neck pain or stiffness (most common physical prodrome — reported in 60–80% of patients) - Shoulder tension - Scalp tenderness (precedes allodynia) **Sensory Sensitivity (Mild, Pre-attack)** - Mild light sensitivity (not yet frank photophobia) - Mild sound sensitivity - Heightened smell sensitivity - Skin hypersensitivity **Gastrointestinal** - Nausea (mild)

- Neck pain or stiffness (most common physical prodrome — reported in 60–80% of patients) - Shoulder tension - Scalp tenderness (precedes allodynia) **Sensory Sensitivity (Mild, Pre-attack)** - Mild light sensitivity (not yet frank photophobia) - Mild sound sensitivity - Heightened smell sensitivity - Skin hypersensitivity **Gastrointestinal** - Nausea (mild) - Loss of appetite or increased appetite - Food cravings — especially chocolate, carbohydrates, salty foods - Thirst changes **Sleep** - Hypersomnia (increased sleep need) - Insomnia - Vivid dreams #### Prodrome Symptom Severity Scale Rate each symptom: 0 = absent, 1 = mild, 2 = moderate, 3 = severe #### Prodrome Symptom Timestamp Protocol - Record time of symptom onset (not just date) - Track progression over hours - Note resolution time (prodrome resolves as headache begins, or overlaps) --- ### Phase 2: Aura **Timing:** Typically 20–60 minutes before or concurrent with headache onset **Prevalence:** ~25–30% of migraineurs experience aura; more common in women Aura results from cortical spreading depression (CSD) — a wave of neuronal depolarization propagating at 2–3 mm/min across the cortex. #### Visual Aura (Most Common — ~99% of aura cases) **Positive Visual Phenomena** - **Scintillating scotoma:** Shimmering, flickering crescent — most characteristic - **Fortification spectra (teichopsia):** Jagged, angular, arc-shaped pattern - **Photopsia:** Flashes of light, stars, sparks - **Geometric patterns:** Zigzag lines, kaleidoscopic patterns **Negative Visual Phenomena** - **Scotoma:** Blank spot in visual field - **Blurring:** Indistinct central or peripheral vision - **Hemianopia:** Loss of half visual field **Characteristics** - Typically begins at center of visual field, expands outward - Duration: 20–60 minutes (diagnostic criterion: 5–60 min) - Fully reversible - Monocular vs. binocular (monocular = retinal migraine, not typical aura) #### Sensory Aura - Paresthesia (tingling, pins-and-needles): typically starts in hand, spreads to arm/face - Numbness - Cheiro-oral spread: hand → arm → face

visual field, expands outward - Duration: 20–60 minutes (diagnostic criterion: 5–60 min) - Fully reversible - Monocular vs. binocular (monocular = retinal migraine, not typical aura) #### Sensory Aura - Paresthesia (tingling, pins-and-needles): typically starts in hand, spreads to arm/face - Numbness - Cheiro-oral spread: hand → arm → face - Unilateral - Duration: 5–60 minutes; fully reversible #### Speech / Language Aura (Dysphasic Aura) - Difficulty finding words (anomia) - Slurred or disorganized speech - Comprehension difficulty - Duration: 5–60 minutes #### Motor Aura (Hemiplegic Migraine — Rare) - Unilateral motor weakness - May last hours to days - Familial or sporadic hemiplegic migraine (FHM/SHM) — genetic basis - **Important:** Must be distinguished from stroke — urgent workup if new onset #### Brainstem Aura (Previously: Basilar Migraine) - Vertigo - Diplopia (double vision) - Tinnitus - Ataxia - Altered consciousness - Bilateral sensory disturbance - Dysarthria - Differentiate from posterior circulation TIA/stroke #### Retinal Migraine - Monocular visual disturbance or temporary monocular vision loss - Must exclude retinal artery occlusion, amaurosis fugax #### Aura Tracking Template | Aura Type | Present | Duration (min) | Laterality | Description | Sequence No. | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Visual | | | | | | | Sensory | | | | | | | Speech | | | | | | | Motor | | | | | | | Brainstem | | | | | | --- ### Phase 3: Headache (Ictal Phase) **Timing:** Onset after prodrome/aura; duration 4–72 hours (untreated) **Core ICHD-3 Criteria Features** #### Pain Characteristics - **Location:** Unilateral (60%) / Bilateral (40%) - Note: Side consistency or side-switching across attacks - **Quality:** Pulsating / throbbing (required for ICHD-3 diagnosis) - **Severity:** Moderate to severe (NRS ≥5) - **Aggravation:** Worsened by routine physical activity (walking, climbing stairs) #### Associated Symptoms

lasts 4–48 hours **Prevalence:** 80% of migraineurs report postdrome symptoms Postdrome arises from sustained cortical and brainstem changes persisting after headache resolves. #### Postdrome Symptoms **Cognitive** - Difficulty concentrating ("brain fog") - Slowed thinking - Memory impairment - Feeling "detached" or dull

4: Postdrome (Migraine Hangover) **Timing:** Follows headache resolution; lasts 4–48 hours **Prevalence:** 80% of migraineurs report postdrome symptoms Postdrome arises from sustained cortical and brainstem changes persisting after headache resolves. #### Postdrome Symptoms **Cognitive** - Difficulty concentrating ("brain fog") - Slowed thinking - Memory impairment - Feeling "detached" or dull **Mood** - Exhaustion / fatigue (most common) - Mild euphoria or well-being (paradoxical; sometimes follows severe attack) - Low mood, depression - Emotional flatness **Physical** - Muscle weakness - Scalp tenderness (resolving allodynia) - Neck stiffness - Sensitivity to head movement **Gastrointestinal** - Nausea (resolving) - Changes in appetite (often increased after attack) #### Postdrome Severity Scoring - Rate overall postdrome severity: 0–10 - Track duration (hours to resolution) - Note functional impairment during postdrome --- ## Symptom Severity and Timing Scales ### Pain Severity Scales | Scale | Range | Use | |---|---|---| | Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) | 0–10 | Universal; simple | | Visual Analog Scale (VAS) | 0–100 mm | Research-grade; continuous | | Verbal Rating Scale (VRS) | None/Mild/Moderate/Severe | Easy for acute documentation | | Faces Pain Scale | 6 faces | Pediatric / low-literacy | ### Functional Impairment Scales **MIDAS (Migraine Disability Assessment) — Quarterly** - 5 questions; score 0–5 (minimal) to ≥21 (severe) - Grade I (0–5): Little or no disability - Grade II (6–10): Mild disability - Grade III (11–20): Moderate disability - Grade IV (≥21): Severe disability **HIT-6 (Headache Impact Test) — Per Attack or Monthly** - 6 items; score 36–78 - ≤49: Little or no impact - 50–55: Some impact - 56–59: Substantial impact - ≥60: Severe impact **PGIC (Patient Global Impression of Change)** - 7-point scale: Much worse → Much better - Used to assess treatment response over time --- ## Multi-Dimensional Symptom Tracking Matrix For each attack,

# Acute Migraine Treatments ## Overview Acute (abortive) migraine treatments are medications and interventions taken at the **onset of a migraine attack** to stop or reduce the severity of the episode. They are not taken daily but used on-demand when an attack begins. Timely administration — ideally within the first 30–60 minutes of symptom onset — is critical for maximum efficacy. Acute treatments are classified into **migraine-specific** (triptans, ditans, gepants, ergotamines) and **non-specific** (NSAIDs, antiemetics, analgesics, opioids) categories. --- ## 1. Migraine-Specific Acute Treatments ### 1.1 Triptans (5-HT1B/1D Receptor Agonists) Triptans are the **gold standard** for moderate-to-severe migraine. They work by constricting cranial blood vessels and inhibiting the release of pro-inflammatory neuropeptides (CGRP, substance P). #### Mechanism of Action - Selective agonists at serotonin 5-HT1B and 5-HT1D receptors - Cause vasoconstriction of dilated intracranial arteries - Inhibit trigeminal nerve activation and neurogenic inflammation - Block pain signal transmission at the trigeminal nucleus caudalis #### Available Triptans | Drug | Route | Onset | Half-life | Notes | |------|-------|-------|-----------|-------| | Sumatriptan | Oral, SC, Nasal, Patch | 30–60 min (oral) | 2 hrs | First-in-class; SC fastest onset (10 min) | | Rizatriptan | Oral, ODT | 30 min | 2–3 hrs | High efficacy; ODT useful with nausea | | Eletriptan | Oral | 30 min | 4 hrs | High efficacy, longer duration | | Zolmitriptan | Oral, Nasal | 45 min | 3 hrs | Nasal useful when vomiting present | | Almotriptan | Oral | 45–60 min | 3–4 hrs | Good tolerability | | Naratriptan | Oral | 1–3 hrs | 6 hrs | Slower onset; lower recurrence; gentle side-effect profile | | Frovatriptan | Oral | 2–4 hrs | 26 hrs | Longest half-life; useful for menstrual migraine | #### Dosing (Standard Adult) - **Sumatriptan**:

| 3–4 hrs | Good tolerability | | Naratriptan | Oral | 1–3 hrs | 6 hrs | Slower onset; lower recurrence; gentle side-effect profile | | Frovatriptan | Oral | 2–4 hrs | 26 hrs | Longest half-life; useful for menstrual migraine | #### Dosing (Standard Adult) - **Sumatriptan**: 50–100 mg oral; 6 mg SC; 5–20 mg nasal - **Rizatriptan**: 5–10 mg oral - **Eletriptan**: 20–40 mg oral - **Frovatriptan**: 2.5 mg oral (menstrual migraine: 2.5 mg BID × 6 days) #### Contraindications - Ischemic heart disease, coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal's angina) - Uncontrolled hypertension - Hemiplegic or basilar migraine - Cerebrovascular disease or peripheral vascular disease - Concurrent MAOI use (serotonin syndrome risk) - Pregnancy (relative contraindication) #### Side Effects - Chest tightness/pressure (non-cardiac), flushing, tingling, dizziness - Triptan sensations: heaviness, warmth in limbs - Medication overuse headache (MOH) if used >10 days/month #### Triptan Non-Responders - ~30–40% of patients do not respond to the first triptan tried - Switching to a different triptan or route of administration is recommended - Combination with an NSAID (e.g., sumatriptan + naproxen) improves outcomes --- ### 1.2 Ditans (5-HT1F Receptor Agonists) #### Lasmiditan (Reyvow) - **Mechanism**: Selective 5-HT1F agonist — no vasoconstriction, neurally-mediated - **Dose**: 50 mg, 100 mg, or 200 mg oral - **Onset**: ~1–1.5 hours - **Key Advantage**: Safe in cardiovascular disease (no vasoconstrictive properties) - **Side Effects**: Dizziness, somnolence, paresthesia, CNS depression - **Warning**: Do not drive for ≥8 hours after taking; Schedule V controlled substance (USA) - **Indication**: Moderate-to-severe migraine with or without aura --- ### 1.3 Gepants (CGRP Receptor Antagonists) Gepants block CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide) at its receptor, targeting the key peptide responsible for migraine pain and vasodilation. #### Available Gepants for Acute Treatment | Drug | Dose | Route | Onset | Notes | |------|------|-------|-------|-------|

Moderate-to-severe migraine with or without aura --- ### 1.3 Gepants (CGRP Receptor Antagonists) Gepants block CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide) at its receptor, targeting the key peptide responsible for migraine pain and vasodilation. #### Available Gepants for Acute Treatment | Drug | Dose | Route | Onset | Notes | |------|------|-------|-------|-------| | Ubrogepant (Ubrelvy) | 50–100 mg | Oral | ~1.5 hrs | Safe with CV disease; no vasoconstriction | | Rimegepant (Nurtec ODT) | 75 mg | ODT | ~1.5 hrs | Dual use: acute + preventive (every other day) | #### Advantages over Triptans - No risk of MOH (medication overuse headache) — key benefit - No vasoconstrictive effects → safe in cardiovascular/cerebrovascular disease - Can be used in hemiplegic migraine #### Side Effects - Nausea, somnolence, dry mouth (generally well-tolerated) #### Drug Interactions - CYP3A4 inhibitors increase drug levels (e.g., ketoconazole, clarithromycin) - Strong CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., rifampin) reduce efficacy --- ### 1.4 Ergotamines (Ergot Alkaloids) Older class; less commonly used due to side effects but still relevant for refractory cases. #### Dihydroergotamine (DHE) - **Routes**: IV, IM, SC, Nasal (Migranal), Inhaled (Trudhesa) - **Mechanism**: Mixed 5-HT, dopamine, and adrenergic agonist; potent vasoconstrictor - **Indication**: Severe, refractory, or prolonged migraine; status migrainosus - **Dose**: 0.5–1 mg IV/IM/SC (can repeat up to 3 mg/day); 0.5 mg intranasal per nostril - **IV Protocol (Raskin Protocol)**: Metoclopramide 10 mg IV + DHE 0.5–1 mg IV q8h × 3 days for status migrainosus - **Side Effects**: Nausea, vomiting (pretreat with antiemetic), peripheral vasoconstriction, ergotism - **Contraindications**: CAD, PVD, uncontrolled HTN, pregnancy, concurrent triptans or CYP3A4 inhibitors #### Ergotamine Tartrate - Oral/sublingual (often combined with caffeine — Cafergot) - Less preferred due to variable absorption and higher side effect profile --- ## 2. # Non-Drug Therapies for Migraine ## Overview Non-pharmacological (non-drug) therapies play a critical and often underutilized role in comprehensive migraine management. They serve as **preventive interventions, acute relief measures, adjuncts to pharmacotherapy, and long-term disease modifiers**. For a RAG-based migraine early warning prediction system, non-drug therapies are especially relevant because many directly target the **neurobiological mechanisms** implicated in migraine prediction — cortical excitability, autonomic dysregulation, circadian rhythm, stress response, and sensory sensitization. Non-drug approaches are classified into: 1. **Neuromodulation devices** 2. **Behavioral and psychological therapies** 3. **Physical therapies and manual interventions** 4. **Lifestyle interventions and trigger management** 5. **Mind-body practices** 6. **Dietary and nutritional approaches** 7. **Complementary and integrative medicine** 8. **Interventional procedures (non-pharmacological component)** --- ## 1. Neuromodulation Devices Neuromodulation is the most evidence-rich non-drug category for migraine, with multiple FDA-cleared devices now available. ### 1.1 Transcutaneous Supraorbital Nerve Stimulation (tSNS) #### Cefaly Device - **Target**: Supraorbital and supratrochlear branches of the ophthalmic nerve (V1 of trigeminal) - **Mechanism**: External electrical stimulation desensitizes trigeminal pain pathways; reduces cortical excitability; modulates thalamo-cortical connectivity - **FDA Status**: FDA-authorized (De Novo) — both acute (2021) and preventive (2014) use - **Preventive Protocol**: 20 minutes daily at 60 Hz, 250 μs pulse width, 16 mA - **Acute Protocol**: 60-minute session at 100 Hz at headache onset - **Efficacy (Preventive)**: ~37–50% reduction in migraine days/month; ~53% responder rate - **Efficacy (Acute)**: ~60% abortive success within 1 hour; reduces need for rescue medication - **Side Effects**: Forehead skin irritation, paresthesia, drowsiness (mild); excellent safety profile - **Contraindications**: Implanted metal/electronic devices in head region - **Patient Profile**: Particularly useful for patients who dislike injections or oral medications - **Relevance to Prediction System**: Cefaly-preventive mode measurably changes cortical excitability — EEG habituation patterns normalize with regular use; baseline excitability state is relevant to predicting breakthrough attacks ---

Complementary and Integrative Medicine ### 7.1 Green Light Therapy - **Evidence**: Emerging (Burstein lab, Harvard); pilot RCTs positive - **Mechanism**: Green light wavelength (~530 nm) uniquely activates intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells in a way that inhibits trigeminal activation and reduces photophobia; narrow-band green light may reduce nociceptor activity - **Protocol**: 1–2 hours daily exposure to pure green light (Allay Lamp); dim otherwise - **Applications**: Both acute (during attack — reduces photophobia) and preventive - **Advantage**: Completely non-pharmacological; safe in all populations including pregnancy ### 7.2 Blue Light Blocking / Light Management - **Photophobia** (light sensitivity) is common interictal and worsens during attacks - Blue light (400–490 nm) maximally stimulates melanopsin (ipRGCs) → activates trigeminovascular pain - **Interventions**: Blue-light blocking glasses (FL-41 tint), screen filters, dimmer lighting environments - **Evidence**: Level B — FL-41 tinted lenses significantly reduce photophobia and migraine frequency ### 7.3 Aromatherapy - **Lavender oil**: Inhaled; RCT showed significant reduction in headache severity during acute migraine - **Peppermint oil**: Topical application (temples, forehead); menthol activates TRPM8 channels → counteracts pain signaling; comparable to acetaminophen in one RCT - **Evidence**: Level C — limited but positive; mechanism-plausible ### 7.4 TENS (Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation) - Different from neuromodulation devices above; portable home TENS units for neck/cervical - **Target**: Cervical nerve roots; reduces referred pain to head via

# Preventive (Prophylactic) Migraine Treatments ## Overview Preventive migraine treatment aims to **reduce the frequency, severity, and duration** of migraine attacks over time. It is distinct from acute treatment and requires daily or regular administration regardless of headache occurrence. Preventive therapy is an essential complement to early warning prediction systems — identifying high-risk windows can help optimize timing and patient adherence, while effective prevention reduces the overall attack burden that prediction systems must manage. --- ## 1. Indications for Preventive Treatment Preventive therapy should be considered when: - **Frequency**: ≥4 migraine days/month - **Duration**: Attacks lasting >24 hours regularly - **Disability**: Significant functional impairment (MIDAS score ≥11, HIT-6 ≥56) - **Acute medication overuse**: Risk or established MOH (medication overuse headache) - **Inefficacy of acute treatments**: Poor/incomplete response to acute medications - **Contraindications to acute therapy**: Patient cannot use triptans (CV disease, hemiplegic migraine) - **Special conditions**: Hemiplegic migraine, migraine with prolonged aura, frequent aura - **Patient preference**: Patient strongly desires fewer attacks ### Rule of Thumb > If a patient uses acute medication ≥2 days/week, preventive therapy is indicated. --- ## 2. General Principles - **Onset of effect**: Most preventive medications require **4–12 weeks** to show full benefit - **Trial duration**: Minimum 3–6 months before declaring treatment failure - **Dose escalation**: Start low, titrate slowly to minimize side effects - **Outcome measure**: Success = ≥50% reduction in migraine days/month - **Patient diary/tracking**: Critical for assessing efficacy and predicting future attacks - **Comorbidity-driven selection**: Choose agents that treat both migraine and comorbid conditions (e.g., topiramate for obesity, amitriptyline for depression, propranolol for hypertension) --- ## 3. CGRP-Targeted Preventive Therapies (Novel) This represents the **most significant advance in migraine prevention in 25 years**. ### 4.1 Anti-CGRP Monoclonal Antibodies (mAbs) CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide) plays a central role in migraine pathophysiology — elevated during attacks, in the trigeminovascular system, and during prodrome phase. #### Anti-CGRP Ligand Antibodies | Drug | Brand | Dose | Route | Frequency | Notes | |------|-------|------|-------|-----------|-------| | Erenumab | Aimovig | 70–140 mg | SC | Monthly | Anti-CGRP *receptor* antibody (unique) | | Fremanezumab | Ajovy | 225 mg or 675 mg | SC | Monthly or quarterly | Anti-CGRP *ligand* | | Galcanezumab | Emgality | 240 mg loading → 120 mg | SC | Monthly | Anti-CGRP ligand; also approved for cluster headache | | Eptinezumab | Vyepti | 100–300 mg IV

# Food Triggers in Migraine: Early Warning Prediction System ## Overview Dietary factors are among the most commonly reported migraine triggers, affecting approximately 20–50% of migraine sufferers. Food triggers can initiate or exacerbate migraines through multiple mechanisms including vasoactive amine release, neuroinflammation, changes in serotonin metabolism, and direct stimulation of trigeminovascular pathways. The onset of a food-triggered migraine typically occurs within **30 minutes to 12 hours** after consumption, though delayed reactions up to 24–48 hours are possible with certain food components. --- ## Mechanism of Food-Triggered Migraines ### 1. Vasoactive Amines Compounds such as **tyramine**, **histamine**, **phenylethylamine**, and **serotonin** found in foods can cause cerebral vasodilation/vasoconstriction and stimulate trigeminal nerve pathways. ### 2. Excitotoxicity **Monosodium glutamate (MSG)** and **aspartame** can overstimulate NMDA receptors in the brain, lowering the migraine threshold. ### 3. Platelet Aggregation & Serotonin Fluctuation Phenylethylamine (in chocolate) promotes platelet aggregation, causing a sudden release of serotonin followed by a sharp drop — a known migraine precipitant. ### 4. Nitric Oxide (NO) Release **Nitrates and nitrites** in cured meats trigger endothelial nitric oxide synthesis, causing vasodilation and headache onset. ### 5. Alcohol-Related Mechanisms Alcohol — particularly **red wine** — contains histamine, tyramine, flavonoids, and sulfites. It also dehydrates the body and causes acetaldehyde accumulation, all of which contribute to migraine. --- ## High-Risk Food Categories ### Alcoholic Beverages | Beverage | Primary Trigger Compounds | |---|---| | Red wine | Histamine, tyramine, sulfites, flavonoids | | Beer | Histamine, tyramine, gluten | | Spirits (whiskey, bourbon) | Congeners, tannins | | Champagne/sparkling wine | Sulfites, rapid CO2-induced vasodilation | **Risk level:** Very High **Onset:** 30 min – 3 hours post-consumption --- ### Aged & Fermented Foods | Food | Primary Trigger Compounds | |---|---| | Aged cheeses (cheddar, blue, parmesan, brie) | Tyramine | | Fermented soy products

# Hormonal Triggers in Migraine: Early Warning Prediction System ## Overview Hormonal fluctuations — particularly involving **estrogen, progesterone, serotonin, cortisol, melatonin, and insulin** — are among the most powerful and consistent migraine triggers. Hormonal migraine affects **up to 60% of women** who experience migraine, with attacks clustered around predictable hormonal events in the reproductive cycle. Hormonal migraines tend to be **longer (up to 72 hours)**, **more severe**, **more resistant to standard treatment**, and more likely to be accompanied by nausea and vomiting than non-hormonal attacks. For a prediction system, hormonal patterns offer high-value **time-predictable signal inputs**, particularly when combined with menstrual cycle tracking data. --- ## Primary Hormonal Mechanisms ### 1. Estrogen Withdrawal The most well-characterized hormonal migraine trigger. **Pathway:** - Estrogen maintains serotonergic tone by upregulating serotonin receptors (5-HT₂) and tryptophan hydroxylase - Estrogen drop → serotonin synthesis decrease → decreased descending pain inhibition → lowered migraine threshold - Estrogen also modulates CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide) release from trigeminal nerve terminals - Falling estrogen → increased CGRP → meningeal vasodilation → trigeminal pain activation **When estrogen drops:** - 2–3 days before menstruation (luteal-to-menstrual transition) - Ovulation (brief mid-cycle estrogen dip) - Perimenopause - Placebo/pill-free week in combined oral contraceptive users - Post-partum estrogen withdrawal - Post-surgical menopause **Critical threshold:** A drop of ≥ **10–25 pg/mL estradiol** within 24–48 hours can precipitate migraine. --- ### 2. Progesterone Effects - High progesterone in the luteal phase has a mild protective effect via GABA-A modulation (anxiolytic, anti-excitatory) - Rapid progesterone fall before menstruation disinhibits excitatory systems - **Net effect:** The combined fall of both estrogen and progesterone just before menstruation is the highest-risk window --- ### 3. Prostaglandins - During menstruation, **prostaglandin E2 (PGE2)** and **PGF2α** released from the uterine endometrium - PGE2 directly sensitizes trigeminal pain fibers and promotes neurogenic inflammation

menstruation disinhibits excitatory systems - **Net effect:** The combined fall of both estrogen and progesterone just before menstruation is the highest-risk window --- ### 3. # Screen & Light Triggers in Migraine: Early Warning Prediction System ## Overview Light sensitivity (**photophobia**) is present in **80–90% of migraine patients** during attacks, and visual stimuli can also *trigger* migraine in a significant subset. Light-related triggers operate through multiple pathways: direct activation of the intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs), cortical hyperexcitability to visual stimulation, melatonin suppression via blue light, and eye strain-related trigeminocervical activation. Digital screen exposure has emerged as a **modern, high-prevalence trigger category** due to increased blue light emission, flicker from displays, prolonged near-focus work, and postural strain. The average person now spends **7–10 hours per day** looking at screens — placing this in the top tier of modifiable trigger exposure. --- ## Anatomy of Light-Mediated Migraine Triggers ### The Retino-Thalamic Pain Pathway 1. **Intrinsically Photosensitive Retinal Ganglion Cells (ipRGCs)** — contain melanopsin; most sensitive to **460–480 nm blue wavelength** light 2. ipRGCs project to the **olivary pretectal nucleus** and **suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)** (circadian pacemaker) 3. Also project to the **posterior thalamus** — which is hyperexcitable in migraineurs 4. Thalamo-cortical projection to visual cortex → abnormally amplified visual processing in migraine brain 5. Thalamo-trigeminal projection → light stimulus activates trigeminal pain pathways (**photophobia mechanism**) > **Key insight:** In migraineurs, the pathway from light stimulus to pain activation is **chronically sensitized**, meaning light triggers that would not affect non-migraineurs can initiate or escalate an attack. ### Cortical Hyperexcitability in Migraineurs - Between attacks, the migraine brain is measurably more reactive to visual stimulation - **Pattern Glare:** Regular visual patterns (stripes, grids, closely spaced lines) at specific spatial frequencies (3 cycles/degree) trigger uncomfortable sensations and can initiate migraine - **Visual Cortex Magnocellular Pathway Defect:** Impaired motion detection processing makes certain visual patterns particularly aversive --- ## Light Trigger Categories ### 1. # Sleep Triggers in Migraine: Early Warning Prediction System ## Overview Sleep disturbances are bidirectionally linked with migraine — they are both a **trigger** and a **consequence** of migraine attacks. Approximately **50% of migraineurs** report sleep problems as a significant trigger, and conversely, migraine pain disrupts healthy sleep in the majority of patients. The relationship is mediated through shared neurological substrates: the hypothalamus, brainstem raphe nuclei, and thalamo-cortical circuits regulate both migraine susceptibility and the sleep-wake cycle. The **most dangerous sleep-related trigger windows** are early morning (4–9 AM), when circadian cortisol surges and REM sleep peaks — a period when over 70% of migraine attacks that begin during sleep occur. --- ## Mechanisms: How Sleep Disruption Triggers Migraine ### 1. Serotonin & Hypothalamic Dysregulation - The **dorsal raphe nucleus** (primary serotonin source) governs both migraine susceptibility and sleep-wake transitions - Sleep deprivation → serotonin synthesis and receptor sensitivity decrease - Low serotonin → increased cortical excitability, lowered migraine threshold - The hypothalamus acts as a "migraine generator" — its disruption through sleep irregularity explains prodromal symptoms (yawning, food cravings, mood changes) 24–48 hours before attack ### 2. Orexin (Hypocretin) System - Orexin-A and Orexin-B neurons in the lateral hypothalamus regulate sleep stability and arousal - Orexin system dysfunction is implicated in both **narcolepsy** and **migraine** - Orexin modulates trigeminal pain transmission; orexin receptor agonists are under investigation as migraine therapeutics - Sleep fragmentation disrupts orexin tone → trigeminal sensitization ### 3. REM Sleep & Migraine Timing - Most sleep-related migraine attacks begin during **REM sleep** or upon awakening from it - During REM: increased cerebral blood flow, variable heart rate, fluctuating cortical activity - REM sleep is rich in cortical spreading depression-like activity in migraine-prone individuals - The longest REM periods occur in the **early morning hours (4–7 AM)** —

attacks begin during **REM sleep** or upon awakening from it - During REM: increased cerebral blood flow, variable heart rate, fluctuating cortical activity - REM sleep is rich in cortical spreading depression-like activity in migraine-prone individuals - The longest REM periods occur in the **early morning hours (4–7 AM)** — explaining early morning migraine onset ### 4. Cortisol Circadian Rhythm - Cortisol rises steeply from ~4–8 AM (the cortisol awakening response, CAR) - This rapid cortisol rise, if timed poorly with sleep disruption, creates a stress-hormone surge that precipitates migraine - Abnormal CAR is documented in chronic migraine patients ### 5. Adenosine Accumulation - Prolonged wakefulness → adenosine buildup → cerebral vasodilation → increased migraine susceptibility - Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, explaining its acute migraine-relieving effect - But caffeine used to compensate for sleep deprivation ultimately disrupts sleep architecture → worsening the cycle --- ## Sleep-Related Migraine Triggers: Classification ### A. Sleep Deprivation (Too Little Sleep) **Definition:** Less than 6 hours in adults (age-adjusted) **Mechanisms:** - Serotonin depletion, cortisol disruption, systemic inflammatory cytokine elevation (IL-6, TNF-α) - Pain threshold decreases measurably after even one night of poor sleep **Clinical patterns:** | Sleep Duration | Migraine Risk | |---|---| | ≥ 8 hours (individual optimal) | Baseline | | 6–7 hours | Mildly elevated | | 5–6 hours | Moderately elevated | | < 5 hours | Very High | | < 4 hours | Extreme; near-certain trigger in susceptible individuals | **Cumulative deficit:** Sleep debt accumulates over multiple nights, not just acute deprivation. A 3-night period of 5-hour sleep (15 hours total lost) carries higher risk than one single night of 3-hour sleep. --- ### B. # Stress Triggers in Migraine: Early Warning Prediction System ## Overview Stress is the **most frequently reported migraine trigger**, cited by 50–80% of migraine patients. The relationship between stress and migraine is bidirectional and complex: stress can trigger migraine attacks, and having migraines is itself a significant source of stress, creating a vicious cycle. Importantly, it is often the **relief after stress** (the "let-down" effect) rather than stress itself that precipitates migraine onset. Stress-related migraine involves the **hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis**, **sympathetic nervous system (SNS)**, **serotonin pathway**, and **neuroinflammatory cascades**, all of which interact with the trigeminal pain system. --- ## Mechanisms: How Stress Triggers Migraine ### 1. HPA Axis Activation & Cortisol Dynamics **During stress:** - Hypothalamus releases **CRH (corticotropin-releasing hormone)** - Pituitary releases **ACTH** - Adrenal glands produce **cortisol** - Elevated cortisol has paradoxical short-term anti-inflammatory effects that can temporarily suppress migraine **After stress (let-down phase):** - Cortisol levels drop rapidly - Immune surveillance rebounds → histamine and inflammatory cytokine release - Serotonin levels destabilize - This post-stress window (typically **24–72 hours** after acute stressor resolves) is peak migraine risk > **"Let-Down Migraine"**: Attacks occurring on weekends, after exams, after project completion, or on the first day of vacation — classic cortisol drop pattern. --- ### 2. Sympathetic Nervous System & Catecholamines - Stress activates **sympathetic nervous system** → release of **adrenaline (epinephrine)** and **noradrenaline (norepinephrine)** - Catecholamines cause vasoconstriction (acute phase) followed by rebound vasodilation - Sustained SNS activation sensitizes the trigeminal vascular system - Norepinephrine depletion after prolonged stress lowers pain threshold --- ### 3. Serotonin Fluctuation - Acute stress triggers a transient serotonin surge - Chronic or repeated stress depletes serotonin stores in raphe nuclei - Low serotonin → reduced descending pain inhibition → central sensitization - Serotonin depletion also promotes cortical spreading depression (CSD) —

prolonged stress lowers pain threshold --- ### 3. # Weather & Environmental Triggers in Migraine: Early Warning Prediction System ## Overview Meteorological and environmental factors are cited as migraine triggers by **50–70% of patients**. Weather changes can precede migraine onset by **6 to 48 hours**, making them highly valuable predictive signals for a real-time warning system. Unlike dietary triggers, weather triggers are external, measurable via APIs, and can be monitored passively without self-reporting. The primary mechanisms involve changes in **barometric pressure**, **temperature differentials**, **humidity**, **wind patterns**, **light intensity**, and **air quality** — all of which affect trigeminal nerve sensitivity, intracranial pressure dynamics, meningeal blood flow, and ion channel activity. --- ## Core Meteorological Triggers ### 1. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ for RAG Retrieval) **Q: Is heat or cold a stronger migraine trigger?** A: Heat is more commonly cited globally, particularly in tropical regions. Cold fronts (rapid temperature drops) are stronger triggers in temperate regions. The rate of temperature change often matters more than the direction or absolute value. **Q: What temperature is too hot and may trigger a migraine?** A: Temperatures above 32°C increase risk; above 36°C, risk is high for susceptible individuals. However, hydration status is the key modifying factor — a well-hydrated person at 38°C has lower risk than a dehydrated person at 33°C. **Q: Why do I get migraines when I come in from the heat to air conditioning?** A: Rapid temperature transition (ΔT of 10–18°C in seconds) triggers vasoconstriction from cold and may directly stimulate trigeminal nerve endings via scalp cold receptors. It is one of the most common urban migraine triggers in hot climates. **Q: Does fever cause migraines?** A: Fever and migraine share overlapping mechanisms (cytokine-induced neuroinflammation, vasodilation) but are distinct. High fever can trigger a migraine attack in susceptible individuals. Treating fever promptly may abort an impending migraine. **Q: How does temperature affect migraine differently in men vs. women?** A: Women generally show greater temperature sensitivity due to estrogen's role in thermoregulation and vascular reactivity. Estrogen fluctuations in the perimenstrual period combined with heat stress create particularly high risk windows. **Q: Can wearing a hat or keeping my head warm reduce cold-triggered migraines?** A: Yes.
